articles.title: Mendonça manda redes apagarem posts associando Flávio Bolsonaro à retirada do posto de padroeira de Nossa Senhora | G1
articles.standfirst: Determinação do ministro detalha posts que devem ser excluídos e atende à decisão tomada pelos ministros no plenário do TSE. Não devem ser removidas publicações apenas com críticas a Flávio.
articles.summary: Determinação do ministro detalha posts que devem ser excluídos e atende à decisão tomada pelos ministros no plenário do TSE. Não devem ser removidas publicações apenas com críticas a Flávio.
articles.body:
O ministro André Mendonça , vice-presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), determinou que as plataformas excluam postagens que atribuam falsamente ao candidato do PL à Presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro , a defesa, articulação, apoio ou compromisso com a retirada de Nossa Senhora Aparecida da condição de padroeira do Brasil.

A determinação foi comunicada nesta sexta-feira (2), após o plenário virtual do TSE ajustar decisão individual de Mendonça.

O ministro havia atendido a um pedido da campanha do parlamentar e determinado a remoção de conteúdos que associassem o senador e sua família ao movimento contrário a Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

A medida provocou uma disputa de liminares no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) antes da análise do caso pelo plenário virtual do TSE.

No ofício, Mendonça esclarece que não devem ser excluídas publicações, por exemplo, que apenas critiquem Flávio Bolsonaro.

“Não deverão, portanto, ser indisponibilizadas publicações em razão da mera proximidade temática, da referência a Nossa Senhora Aparecida, da formulação de críticas ao candidato ou à sua família, da manifestação de caráter religioso ou político, ou de outras circunstâncias que, isoladamente, não importem reprodução do referido núcleo factual”, escreveu o ministro.

André Mendonça no TSE — Foto: Leobark Rodrigues/Secom/TSE

Mendonça afirmou ainda que, em caso de dúvida sobre o conteúdo, a publicação deve ser preservada, sem prejuízo de eventual questionamento à Justiça Eleitoral.

“Em especial, deverão os provedores, à luz dos parâmetros fixados pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, proceder à revisão das medidas adotadas ou que venham a ser adotadas em cumprimento à ordem judicial, observando-se interpretação estrita de seu alcance e, em situações de dúvida razoável quanto ao enquadramento de determinada publicação, privilegiando-se a liberdade de expressão”, afirmou.

articles.title: Presión máxima sobre Pedro Sánchez para que adelante las elecciones ante el probable rechazo de los decretos de vivienda
articles.standfirst: La eventual derrota del Gobierno en el Congreso este viernes podría precipitar el final de la XV Legislatura y abrir la puerta a unos comicios, cuya primera fecha posible sería el 29 de noviembre
articles.summary: La eventual derrota del Gobierno en el Congreso este viernes podría precipitar el final de la XV Legislatura y abrir la puerta a unos comicios, cuya primera fecha posible sería el 29 de noviembre
articles.body: La posibilidad de un adelanto de las elecciones generales ha cobrado fuerza ante el riesgo de que el Congreso de los Diputados rechace este viernes los dos decretos sobre vivienda aprobados por el Consejo de Ministros. El rechazo anunciado por Junts, sumado a la oposición de PP, Vox y UPN, ha elevado la presión sobre Pedro Sánchez, aunque desde Moncloa niegan que se esté preparando una convocatoria electoral y aseguran que la prioridad sigue siendo lograr la convalidación de las medidas. El escenario político se ha complicado después de que Junts confirmara su voto en contra de los decretos. El Gobierno ha decidido mantenerlos en el Pleno y que cada grupo parlamentario se retrate con su voto, en una votación que PSOE y Sumar han forzado que se realice de manera individual. Mientras tanto, en el Ejecutivo crece la percepción de que una derrota parlamentaria podría marcar el final de la actual legislatura. Pedro Sánchez ha insistido hasta ahora en que las elecciones generales se celebrarán en 2027. Sin embargo, algunas fuentes citadas en el entorno político consideran que el rechazo de los decretos podría modificar ese escenario y abrir la puerta a una convocatoria anticipada. La decisión, en cualquier caso, corresponde exclusivamente al presidente del Gobierno. Desde Moncloa niegan que se esté preparando un adelanto electoral y desmienten que se haya convocado un gabinete de crisis para abordar esa posibilidad. El ministro de Política Territorial y Memoria Democrática, Ángel Víctor Torres, ha rechazado este viernes hacer "cábalas" sobre una eventual disolución de las Cortes y ha defendido que el debate debe centrarse en el derecho a la vivienda. La tensión se produce además en un contexto de fuerte movilización social en torno al acceso a la vivienda, con protestas como la acampada instalada durante varios días en la Puerta del Sol tras el desahucio de una vecina de 87 años del barrio de Retiro. El Gobierno ha utilizado esta situación para reclamar a los grupos de la oposición que permitan mantener las medidas, entre ellas las destinadas a impedir determinados desahucios. El Partido Popular es la formación que se ha mostrado más favorable a la posibilidad de poner fin anticipadamente a la legislatura. Fuentes de la dirección nacional han señalado que el partido está preparado para afrontar unos comicios inmediatos y considera que unas elecciones permitirían a los ciudadanos pronunciarse sobre la situación política actual. El presidente de la Junta de Andalucía, Juanma Moreno, ha reclamado directamente a Pedro Sánchez que disuelva las Cortes y convoque elecciones si los decretos de vivienda son rechazados. Moreno ha comparado la votación con una "moción de confianza", al considerar que serviría para comprobar el respaldo parlamentario real del Ejecutivo. También la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha apuntado a la posibilidad de que se esté preparando el terreno para unas elecciones, en un contexto marcado por la creciente tensión política. Dentro del Gobierno, Sumar mantiene una posición más prudente. La vicepresidenta segunda y ministra de Trabajo, Yolanda Díaz, ha evitado valorar un posible adelanto y ha insistido en que la prioridad debe ser encontrar soluciones al problema de la vivienda. El ministro de Cultura, Ernest Urtasun, ha anunciado que Sumar se reunirá durante el fin de semana si los decretos no son convalidados para analizar la situación y tomar decisiones. El ministro de Derechos Sociales, Pablo Bustinduy, ha recordado que la convocatoria electoral es una competencia exclusiva del presidente del Gobierno, aunque ha asegurado que su espacio político está preparado para cualquier escenario. Desde Podemos, Ione Belarra tampoco ha descartado que Pedro Sánchez pueda convocar elecciones si considera que la decisión le beneficia electoralmente. Al mismo tiempo, ha defendido que las movilizaciones sociales están reclamando soluciones en materia de vivienda y no una convocatoria electoral. El líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, ha defendido que las elecciones se convoquen "cuanto antes", aunque ha reclamado que sean "transparentes y libres". En sus declaraciones ante los medios, Abascal ha lanzado además duras acusaciones contra Sánchez en relación con un eventual adelanto electoral. En el ámbito nacionalista, el PNV ha considerado que un eventual rechazo de los decretos supondría un golpe para la legislatura, aunque su portavoz en el Parlamento Vasco, Joseba Díez Antxustegi, ha evitado anticipar qué consecuencias debería tener esa derrota. Coalición Canaria, por su parte, sí ha defendido abiertamente la convocatoria de elecciones. Su diputada Cristina Valido ha argumentado que carece de sentido prolongar una legislatura en la que los grupos no son capaces de alcanzar acuerdos estables. Si Pedro Sánchez decidiera finalmente disolver las Cortes, la primera fecha posible para celebrar las elecciones generales sería el domingo 29 de noviembre. El calendario electoral establece que, para que la votación se celebre un domingo, la convocatoria debe publicarse un martes en el Boletín Oficial del Estado y la jornada electoral debe tener lugar 54 días después. Para llegar a esa fecha, el Consejo de Ministros tendría que aprobar la disolución de las Cortes en una reunión extraordinaria el lunes y publicar el decreto de convocatoria al día siguiente. Las candidaturas se presentarían entre el 21 y el 26 de octubre, serían proclamadas el 2 de noviembre y la campaña electoral comenzaría el 13 de noviembre. La campaña se prolongaría hasta el 27 de noviembre, mientras que el sábado 28 sería la jornada de reflexión y el domingo 29 se celebrarían las elecciones. Si la decisión se retrasara, el calendario podría desplazarse varios meses para evitar que una campaña electoral coincidiera con el periodo navideño. De momento, el desenlace depende de la votación de los decretos de vivienda y, sobre todo, de la decisión que adopte Pedro Sánchez ante un eventual rechazo parlamentario. La Moncloa mantiene públicamente que el Ejecutivo está centrado en sacar adelante las medidas, mientras los principales partidos ya contemplan escenarios políticos diferentes para las próximas semanas.

articles.title: Democrats regain ground on voter registration in key states after steep post-2024 drops
articles.summary: An NBC News Decision Desk analysis of voter file data in seven states found that Democrats managed to reverse or slow their registration decline over the past year.
articles.body: After having suffered massive voter registration losses in the wake of the last presidential election, Democrats have stemmed the bleeding in several key states heading into this year’s midterms, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis. NBC News’ Decision Desk analyzed voter file data from TargetSmart, a progressive data firm, for seven of the states that were the closest in the 2024 election and that registered voters by party: Arizona, Maine, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina and Pennsylvania. From late 2024 through late 2025, Republicans significantly improved their voter registration margin over Democrats in all seven states, including by a net of roughly 100,000 in Pennsylvania and North Carolina. But from late 2025 through the middle of this year, Democrats managed to reverse, though not completely erase, those losses in five of them, adding more registrants on net than Republicans in Arizona, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. And in New Hampshire and North Carolina, Democrats have slowed the decline. While party registration is not 100% predictive of vote choice, the recent movement toward Democrats on this front provides another reason for optimism for the party this fall. Arizona, Maine, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina and Pennsylvania are all holding critical races for the Senate or governor (if not both), while New Jersey, which has become more competitive in recent years, is hosting a battleground House contest. The trend comes not only amid a backlash to President Donald Trump that has grown over the course of the year, but also as Democrats campaigned in consequential primaries that often centered on what direction the party would take after its 2024 defeat. Meanwhile, the pool of unaffiliated voters continued to expand in many of those states, reflecting a growing distrust of both major parties. There are three primary ways the party registration margin can change: new voters signing up; registrants switching parties; or registrants being removed from the rolls after having moved out of state, routine maintenance or dying. A total of 30 states and Washington, D.C., register voters by party, while the rest — including battlegrounds like Georgia, Michigan and Wisconsin — do not. To track recent voter registration trends, NBC News analyzed TargetSmart data after the 2024 election, at the end of 2025 and in mid-2026, with the most recently available data in each state ranging from late June to September. Democrats’ biggest post-2024 issue on this front largely came from voters leaving the rolls. But the analysis of the voter registration data reveals that the problem was not as severe for Democrats as it might appear, as many of those people were infrequent voters to begin with. In all seven states, turnout in the 2024 election was significantly lower among the people who subsequently left the rolls than among those who stayed. For example, in Pennsylvania, the 2024 turnout among people who subsequently left the rolls was 37%, compared with 81% for those who stayed. In battleground Pennsylvania, Republicans had their biggest net gain in voter registration (more than 110,000) from late 2024 to late 2025 of the seven states analyzed. But from the end of last year to this summer, Democrats gained a net of around 46,000. Despite those big 2025 losses, Democrats actually gained around 22,000 registrants from new voters over that period. But that was offset by net losses from party registration switches (about 43,000) and registrants leaving the rolls (about 90,000). It all adds up in a state Trump won by 120,000 votes in 2024. The data through this fall tells a different story, though. New registrants and party switchers gave Democrats net gains of around 45,000 and 11,000, respectively. That was more than enough to make up for more modest losses among registrants leaving the voter rolls. Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale said he aggressively prioritized voter registration efforts when he took over in September 2025. About 150 staffers are now “having conversations with people in every single corner of our commonwealth, listening to their concerns, listening to their issues and making a case of why they should register as Democrats,” he said, while also crediting Trump’s growing unpopularity. North Carolina, however, has remained a bright spot for the GOP: For the first time in the state’s history, the party holds a lead in party registration. From late 2024 to late 2025, Republicans’ net voter registration gain was just shy of 100,000. Democrats managed to keep the net loss to around 16,000 from late 2025 to last month. “Traditionally, the Democrats have always just been better at this than Republicans,” said Felice Pete, a Republican National Committee member from North Carolina. But in recent years, she said, conservative groups like Turning Point USA and Americans for Prosperity helped Republicans in the state boost their registration numbers through door-knocking and events. “It’s almost like evangelizing, if you will,” she said. Below the surface, there is a promising trend for Democrats in North Carolina. While new registrants gave Republicans a net gain of around 11,000 last year, they gave Democrats a net gain of around 6,000 this year. In North Carolina and four of the other states analyzed — Arizona, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania — the number of people who either did not register with a party or registered with a party that was not the Democrats or the Republicans steadily grew from late 2024 to mid-2026. In Maine and New Jersey, that percentage slightly declined. A significantly larger number of new voters in all seven states are registering as unaffiliated compared than are those currently on the rolls. And much of the movement away from the Democratic Party is from Democrats choosing to become unaffiliated, rather than registering as Republicans.

articles.title: Congress will take your money, they just won’t take care of it like they should
articles.summary: Congress oversees a $7 trillion annual budget and $40 trillion national debt yet has no legal fiduciary duty to act in Americans' interests.
articles.body: The people who oversee the largest budget in the world, who are in charge of an entity ultimately responsible for the largest number of employees in the U.S., and who are put in charge specifically to represent constituents somehow have no broad fiduciary duty — Congress. In most large businesses, and certainly every publicly traded one, a board of directors is put in place to represent that business’s stakeholders. This is referred to as a fiduciary duty, which, in layman’s terms, is a legal obligation to act in the best interests of those you represent. It also comes with consequences, because as a fiduciary, you can be sued for putting your interests ahead of those you represent or for negligence or bad judgment. Fiduciary relationships come into place not only in companies, but for certain financial advisory relationships and trustees as well. The fiduciary relationship is a legal one, which means those in charge must legally act honestly and with care, avoid conflicts of interest and be trustworthy to the parties they represent. EX-HOUSE DEM WHO RIPPED CONGRESSIONAL STOCK TRADING BAN AS 'BULLS---' CHANGES HER TUNE IN COMEBACK BID Somehow, Congress has managed to avoid this. Sure, they take a "moral" oath and have some fairly weak, in my opinion, disclosure and ethics rules. But the people who are in charge of making laws and passing budgets (if you can call regular and overwhelming overspending a "budget") have no true legal, fiduciary role. We have seen and paid the price for this. The national debt exceeds $40 trillion. Congress spends around $7 trillion a year, $2 trillion more than it takes in. They have been at the center of driving massive inflation for the American people. We, as a country, are now paying more for the interest on our debt than we are for the defense of our country, the latter being one legitimate thing government should be doing. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' We have seen Congress write and pass laws that tip the scales in favor of certain groups at the expense of others. We have seen them enrich themselves through stock trading (despite the STOCK Act of 2012). We have seen calls for term limits, an issue which the majority of Americans favor, be ignored, sometimes even leaving members of Congress with clearly diminished capacity in their roles. As I have written about previously, I am often asked if the national debt crisis is solvable. And the answer comes always in two parts: we do have the tools to do so, but we do not have the political structure to do so. If Congress has no obligation to do what is in our best interest instead of theirs, if we cannot hold them accountable for misdeeds, and if our only real recourse is threatening to vote them out of office, nothing is going to change. CONGRESS MUST PASS MY SIX PENNY PLAN It is truly not right that those who act in the capacity of others on serious legal and financial matters in the private sector have a fiduciary obligation to those they represent, yet the behemoth that our government has become bears no such obligation, including from those who represent the American people. articles.title: I saw the real DOGE from the inside. Why the media got DOGE and Elon all wrong
articles.summary: A former DOGE lead at the Department of the Interior describes Elon Musk's relentless work ethic and defends the team against media caricatures.
articles.body: My book about my time inside DOGE launched last week, and I've watched friends who privately cheer me on go completely silent in public. That’s how toxic the stigma around DOGE has become. And that stigma is built on a version of events I barely recognize. My experience inside DOGE was almost nothing like what I read about in the mainstream news. The fairest and most balanced coverage I can remember was our interview on Fox News with Bret Baier in March 2025 — but let me tell you what it was actually like. As the DOGE lead and acting assistant secretary for the U.S. Department of the Interior, I saw the accusations that we cut everything indiscriminately. That could not be further from the truth. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE Along with my DOGE colleagues and the incredible leadership of Secretary Doug Burgum, we went through thousands of contracts and grants ourselves and asked the people who knew them best to help us. Our request was simple: "Defend the spend" and tell us what was "mission-critical." If a contract couldn't be defended, or even explained, why were hardworking Americans paying for it? We cut what didn't make sense and made individuals accountable. Then there's the claim that we didn't respect career civil servants. That wasn't my experience either. I have tremendous respect for the many hardworking, genuine and intelligent people who serve in government. Many are friends of mine today. THE US HAS A $40 TRILLION DEBT CRISIS. BILLIONAIRE WARREN BUFFET KNOWS HOW TO SOLVE IT What shocked me wasn't the people — it was the system around them: the inefficient organizations, the decades-old technology and the near-total absence of accountability. Many good people were trapped inside a machine built to resist common sense. Did we get along with everyone? No. We were there to challenge the mindset that "this is how it's always been done" as stewards of the American taxpayer. We intentionally disrupted a culture that had grown comfortable with the status quo — and yes, that made some jobs less comfortable. That was the point. Americans work hard for those dollars and deserve a government that spends them prudently. Some conflict was inevitable. But I left Washington with far more respect for career government workers than I expected to have. What shocked me wasn't the people — it was the system around them: the inefficient organizations, the decades-old technology and the near-total absence of accountability. Many good people were trapped inside a machine built to resist common sense. What about the caricature of reckless "DOGE bros" running wild? First, those young engineers are some of the brightest people in this country. They are great Americans who sacrificed enormous private-sector opportunities to put their talents to work for their love of country. Second, the caricature erases the roughly 20 brilliant women on our team, three of them on mine at Interior. Did they want to step into the spotlight amid all the media hostility? Of course not — I feared for my own family's safety and theirs. They did it anyway and kept working relentlessly to reduce the deficit and help American families. And our leadership? I keep hearing people ask how anyone could work for someone as volatile as Elon Musk. I saw the opposite. I saw a man so locked in on the problem that he sometimes slept on the floor in a nearby office. In our meetings, two things struck me that I'll never forget: his ability to be completely present with a problem until it was solved, and a sense of urgency so strong that everyone in the room felt it. When the criticism got louder, we worked harder. I wish more Americans could have seen the teamwork and the love of country in those rooms. Despite our best efforts, we didn't accomplish all that we set out to do. But we tried harder than anyone outside those rooms will ever know — and we proved something that matters. We proved that the operations of our government have enormous room for improvement and that talented people willing to do the work can find problems and fix them. That's exactly why treating DOGE as a failure to be buried is the wrong lesson. The right lesson is to learn from it and build something better. articles.title: How a hidden scam plaguing college campuses has racked up a multimillion-dollar price tag
articles.summary: A fraud expert reveals the red flags students and parents must watch for as ghost students drain millions from the federal student aid system.
articles.body: A hidden scheme draining millions from the federal student aid system and infiltrating college campuses has emerged as a key target of the Trump administration's fraud crackdown, with officials faulting Biden-era identity verification policies for opening the door to it. One fraud expert is now highlighting the red flags students and parents must look out for as the fall semester begins, warning fraudsters are fabricating identities to enroll at colleges and collect aid that is meant for legitimate students. "People, scammers specifically, look for vulnerable places like student loans and unemployment fraud to take advantage of those channels because historically they have been lax in their controls," Mallory Wortman, senior fraud investigator at financial crime prevention firm Abrigo, told Fox News Digital. In June, the Education Department also said it saved taxpayers nearly $200 million after requiring high-risk applicants to present government-issued identification when applying for federal student aid, Fox News Digital previously reported. The identity verification system was integrated into the online FAFSA application, with department officials estimating it will save taxpayers more than $1 billion this cycle. STOLEN IDS SOLD FOR ‘HAPPY MEAL’ PRICES FUEL BILLIONS IN US BENEFIT FRAUD The department took aim at weak fraud safeguards under former President Joe Biden, accusing his administration of requiring less than 1% of students to verify their identity following their FAFSA submission during the COVID-19 pandemic era. The administration has also paired those safeguards with new enforcement efforts. Vice President JD Vance recently announced that more than 870,000 borrowers tied to alleged COVID-era fraud would be suspended from future federal loan programs, saying they could ultimately face federal prosecution. But the crackdown reflects a simple reality, according to Wortman, who said fraudsters are quick to take advantage of any opportunity where government money is flowing. "Anytime there's an opportunity where funds are flowing, like financial aid fraud, or another example would be when there's unemployment fraud during COVID, they're gonna use that as a method to get those funds," Wortman said. Wortman said fraudsters frequently use so-called "ghost students" to exploit the programs. A "ghost student" is a stolen or fake identity, sometimes created with artificial intelligence (AI), used to enroll in college and collect federal student aid funds, loans or grants. EXPLOSIVE REPORT FINDS $230M IN ALLEGED K-12 EDUCATION FRAUD AMID TRUMP'S CRACKDOWN: 'ESPECIALLY HIDEOUS' She compared the trick to her own time in community college, where she said she watched students enroll, walk away with a financial aid "refund," then suddenly drop out of classes. "That's kind of what we've seen, straw student schemes turning into today," she said, adding today's fraudsters' main objective is "attaining the aid rather than pursuing an education." As students return to campus, Wortman said there are many signs to look out for. "They’re going to have multiple applications," she said. "They're going to have common information. There's gonna be some unusual enrollment patterns and then suspicious changes to their account before those funds are disbursed." Similar "connections and patterns" can also be spotted in banking records, where Wortman described how fraudsters use elaborate data breaches and phishing messages to trick victims into providing personal information. "You're going to have shared information, that unusual movement of funds and then multiple apparently unrelated customers with common either connection activity, IP addresses, and then funds flowing through the account that just don't make sense," she said. TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE According to Wortman, the best defense against these fraudsters starts with keeping a close eye on your personal financial information. "Just be aware and keep tabs on your personal financial information," she said. Despite the heightened focus on the fraud, Wortman said the scam is nothing new and that she is "glad" it is finally being recognized and prevented. The size of the scam became clear last year when the Education Department revealed it blocked more than $1 billion in fraudulent student aid and identified nearly $90 million that had already been fraudulently disbursed. More than $30 million went to deceased individuals, while more than $40 million went to companies using bots disguised as fake students. articles.title: A must-win midterm state is the real loser of Trump's Canada trade war
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada could raise vehicle prices at Michigan dealerships as auto parts cross the border multiple times.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's escalating trade fight with Canada could deliver an economic blow to one of the country's most closely watched battleground states, potentially raising costs for automakers and prices for consumers. Michigan, home to a fiercely contested U.S. Senate race this November, is particularly vulnerable because its auto industry depends heavily on a cross-border supply chain with Canada. America's northern neighbor received roughly $21.2 billion worth of Michigan exports in 2025, about 36% of the state's total, mainly vehicles and parts, according to the Michigan Department of Transportation. David Clement, policy director of the free market nonprofit Consumer Choice Center, warned the costs of tariffs could ultimately reach Michigan drivers. "How you see this as a Michigan consumer is higher prices on the dealership lot," Clement told Fox News Digital, describing tariffs alongside already-elevated living costs as a "double whammy." 5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS Those concerns come as Trump has intensified his trade dispute with Canada. He imposed an additional 50% tariff on certain Canadian products earlier this year, and the administration has since barred certain Canadian products from entering the U.S. beginning Sept. 29. Clement said Michigan ranks among the states most exposed to the dispute. "Michigan, in terms of ranking all of the states in their export vulnerability in the trade war, sits at around seventh," he said, pointing to equipment, machinery and the auto industry as areas of concern. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE That vulnerability is compounded by how frequently auto parts cross the border before a vehicle is completed. "Most Americans don't know that a single component on a U.S.-assembled vehicle can cross the border upwards of eight times before it's actually completed," Clement said. "When you are tariffing automotive parts going across the border each way, that is where the exposure numbers start to tick up," he added, warning that tariffs and retaliation can "really gum up the very intertwined supply chain for cars between Michigan and Ontario." The economic stakes come as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers compete for the Senate seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. Even as the trade fight creates potential political risks in Michigan, the Trump administration has defended its actions as necessary to protect American businesses and workers and level the playing field with Canada. THE FED JUST THREW A WRENCH IN TRUMP'S MIDTERM ECONOMIC MESSAGE Clement, however, argued the dispute could put pressure on American businesses at a politically sensitive time. "It would appear that Donald Trump's original escalation against Canada has somewhat backfired in terms of the midterms," Clement said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He warned that businesses dependent on Canadian goods could feel the effects just as voters head to the polls. "American manufacturers or American businesses who rely on Canadian inputs are going to start to feel the pain right in the lead-up to going to the ballot box," Clement said. "Cost of living, cost of goods, cost of doing business is such an important factor for Americans who are going to be casting a ballot."

articles.title: Ms Rachel builds sprawling media empire while shelling out thousands to progressive candidates
articles.summary: Ms. Rachel has donated thousands to progressive political candidates as her popular children's education brand expanded into Netflix, Penguin Random House and Target.
articles.body: The popular children's YouTuber Rachel Accurso has spent over $22,000 backing Democratic and progressive candidates since 2024, while her toddler-facing brand has expanded into Netflix, Penguin Random House and the toy aisles of Target. Better known as "Ms. Rachel," the online star has cemented herself as the face of a multimillion-dollar children’s entertainment empire. The former New York City preschool educator, who sings nursery rhymes and teaches language to more than 21 million YouTube subscribers, has also become one of the most politically outspoken figures in her arena, drawing scrutiny for her positions on the Israel-Hamas war, racial issues and various Trump administration immigration policies. "Ms. Rachel is a children's entertainer, a personality that spawned from the YouTube ecosystem and has now become a fixture alongside other big preschool brands like Sesame Street or Bluey or Cocomelon," James Zahn, editor-in-chief of "The Toy Book," told Fox News Digital. "For families that have ‘littles,’ as she would say, she's a part of daily life at this point," he added. MS RACHEL URGES 'EVERY WEALTHY WHITE CELEBRITY' TO MATCH MACKLEMORE'S DONATION TO PALESTINIAN CAUSES Accurso, 43, launched her YouTube channel in 2019 after finding few media resources for her son, who had a speech delay as a toddler. Her channel quickly surged in popularity, leading her to create "Songs for Littles," a recurring series in which Accurso — clad in her signature pink shirt, overalls and headband — performs a mix of classic and original children's songs for infants, toddlers and preschoolers. Her rise to fame has made her one of the most commercially significant figures in American children’s media — and, at the same time, one of the most politically outspoken. According to federal records, Accurso has donated roughly $22,500 to various Democratic and progressive candidates since 2024, and has made headlines for her outspoken stances on the Israel-Hamas war and other politically charged topics. MOMS FOR LIBERTY CO-FOUNDER WARNS PARENTS ABOUT MS RACHEL’S POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ‘NOT MR ROGERS’ Accurso has managed to secure deals with Netflix, Penguin Random House Books and Spin Master Toys. "These companies look at it as: if an entertainer doesn't blur real life into the content, that tends to make things a little bit safer," Zahn said. Earlier this year, Spin Master debuted a line of toys in collaboration with Accurso — marking yet another feather in her cap as her brand hit the shelves of big-box stores such as Target and Amazon. "In the years leading up to the announcement of Ms. Rachel's toy deal with Spin Master, there was a bidding war," Zahn said. "So toy and game makers knew that she was a personality with a ton of reach that was worth talking to." MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER "I distinctly remember at Toy Fair New York knowing that Ms. Rachel was in the building — not in character, but she was taking meetings," he continued. "And eventually the question became, within the industry: who is going to get the Ms. Rachel toys?" The line features a variety of toys geared toward both learning and entertainment, with Ms. Rachel personified as a toy-version of herself in several sets. Her reach has also spread from the online ecosystem into both mainstream and print media after she landed partnerships with Netflix in 2025 and book publisher Penguin Random House in 2024. "The Ms. Rachel deal with Netflix brings her show to kids who may not otherwise have access to it," Zahn said. "Even though we're in such a screen-heavy world, not every family allows their kids to operate on YouTube." KAROL MARKOWICZ: MS. RACHEL SAID, 'I AM POLITICAL.' PARENTS SHOULD TAKE HER AT HER WORD "When we think of media, and we think how digital it is, the analog basis — especially for the younger kids — is very, very key," he added, referring to Accurso’s line of children’s books. The multi-pronged licensing approach to Accurso’s brand marks a significant — and somewhat unprecedented — shift in children’s entertainment, in which influencers reign in spaces traditionally reserved for mainstream media. "Today's children, even from the youngest ages, don't just want to watch a television program," David Kleeman, senior vice president of global trends for Dubit, told Fox News Digital. "They want to be part of the media that they consume. They want to play with it. They want to act it out. They want to wear the clothing." As Accurso’s persona continues to reach into every aspect of a child’s life — from the shows they watch to the toys they play with — Kleeman emphasizes the need for the individual behind the brand to maintain a level of trust with the parents choosing to keep her content in the hands of their children. MS RACHEL CLAIMS CELEBRITIES SILENT ON GAZA WOULD ‘PROBABLY’ SPEAK IF CHILDREN ‘WERE WHITE’ "Parents have always looked to media as a support for what they’re doing with their kids," Kleeman said. "We tell parents, ‘You’re your child’s first teacher.’ That petrifies a lot of parents, so [they] look for ways to supplement what [they’re] able to do for your child." However, Accurso’s public politics have made her children’s education brand synonymous with hot-button political issues, such as the ongoing Israel-Hamas war and tensions surrounding Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She's also put some money behind prominent Democrats. In 2024, the day after then-President Joe Biden dropped out of the ongoing election and endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris as his Democratic successor, Accurso donated $250 to the Harris Victory Fund. HOW MS RACHEL'S POLITICAL ACTIVISM IS SPARKING PUSHBACK FROM PARENTS In the days following, she contributed an additional $750 in funds to Harris for President and the Harris Victory Fund, according to Federal Election Commission records. By September 2024, Accurso had shelled out an additional $2,000 in donations to Harris’ campaign — bringing the total to $3,000 in campaign contributions, records show. One year later, Accurso made a $5,000 donation to Cameron Kasky’s New York congressional campaign, according to NYC Campaign Finance Board records obtained by Fox News Digital. She was issued a $1,500 refund from Kasky’s campaign on the same day. Kasky — a survivor of the 2018 high school mass shooting in Parkland, Florida — ran on a platform centered around abolishing ICE, ending military funding to Israel and stricter gun-violence laws. He ultimately dropped out of the race in January 2026 following a trip to the West Bank, in which he cited a new focus on stopping "settler violence" in the region, according to an X post. Throughout 2026, campaign finance records show Accurso has spent $12,000 on various New York races with candidates of similar views. MS RACHEL DEFENDS 'AWESOME' MAMDANI AMID 9/11 MEMORIAL CONTROVERSY, SAYS HE'S VICTIM OF ISLAMOPHOBIC ATTACKS The children’s educator donated $5,000 to former New York State Assemblymember Yuh-Line Niou’s state Senate campaign, plus an additional $3,500 to Democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier and $4,500 to former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander. While Niou failed to win in the primaries earlier this year, both Chevalier and Lander won the Democratic nominations for their respective congressional campaigns. All three candidates have strongly campaigned on platforms that are critical of both Israel and ICE. Federal Election Commission records also show Accurso gave $3,000 to Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan Senate campaign in July, marking yet another contribution to a controversial candidate who has repeatedly alleged Israel is committing a "genocide" in Gaza. DAVID MARCUS: IN BOOMING DETROIT, VOTERS SKEPTICAL OF SOCIALISM SNAKE OIL "I am political," she said in March, describing her opposition to Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She has been similarly direct about the Israel-Hamas war, drawing scrutiny in 2025 after appearing in a video referring to Palestinian photojournalist Motaz Azaiza as her "friend" — days before Azaiza admitted to withholding footage of Israeli hostages being beaten by a crowd in Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023. "There isn't a lot of precedent when it comes to a kid's entertainer making comments outside of their content that rub people the wrong way — or in some cases the right way," Zahn said. The YouTuber’s checkbook tells a similar story, with her net worth reportedly estimated at around $50 million. Last year, Forbes’ 2025 Top Creators List ranked Accurso at No. 20 with a whopping $23 million in annual earnings. The dollar figures — and subsequent brand deals — signify an apparent fan separation between Ms. Rachel as a brand and Accurso as a public figure. "It's always an issue when you have a presenter who is basically presenting as themselves," Kleeman told Fox News Digital. "Mr. Rogers just was ‘Mr. Rogers.’ There was no character or artifice there. Ms. Rachel has created ‘Ms. Rachel,’ as opposed to Rachel Accurso." "Viewers often have a problem separating that real-life person from the character," he added. MS RACHEL CLAIMS 'NO ONE NEEDS A BILLION DOLLARS,' ENDORSES DEMOCRATIC PROGRESSIVES ABDUL EL-SAYED, CORI BUSH The sentiment was echoed by Zahn, who suggests that Accurso’s high-profile political stances are doing little to deter brands from signing her YouTube persona. "Companies can take multiple approaches, as we've seen with other celebrity controversies," Zahn said. "They can choose to back the celebrity, they can push back from the celebrity, they can distance themselves from it, or they can say nothing at all. And sometimes saying nothing at all is what it really needs." While parents may be keyed into Accurso’s views on topics such as Gaza and gender representation, Kleeman argues that as long as the content creator keeps politics out of her educational materials, she will likely feel little pushback from both brands and fans. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I think she's been very careful to keep what she puts out to children focused on the child development, on the learning, on the play," Kleeman told Fox News Digital. "I think that Netflix or any channel that’s carrying content that’s being presented by a real person is going to have to balance how well that person is conveying what it is they’re transmitting to kids — the specific children’s content, not the things that go around it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Accurso, Netflix, Penguin Random House and Spin Master for comment.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: 128 GOP lawmakers call for federal probe into Planned Parenthood's taxpayer funding
articles.summary: A coalition of 128 Republican lawmakers is urging the HHS Inspector General to review Planned Parenthood's federal funding for potential fraud or abuse.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A coalition of 128 Republican lawmakers is pressing the federal government to scrutinize Planned Parenthood's taxpayer funding and potentially launch an investigation into the organization and its affiliates. Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J., and Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., led the bicameral effort, asking Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Inspector General T. March Bell to review Planned Parenthood's federal funding and determine whether the organization and its affiliates have complied with federal laws and funding requirements. "We write to request that the Office of Inspector General (OIG) review and, if appropriate, initiate an investigation into the activities of Planned Parenthood Federation of America, Inc. and the organization's affiliates," the lawmakers wrote. READ: DR. OZ PUTS ALL 50 GOVERNORS ON NOTICE OVER BILLIONS LOST TO MEDICAID FRAUD Their request casts a rather wide net. The lawmakers want the OIG to scrutinize funding flowing through HHS programs, grants, contracts and sub-awards and determine whether evidence exists of fraud, waste, abuse, misrepresentation or other violations affecting federal health programs. If misconduct is uncovered, they want the watchdog to consider consequences ranging from administrative remedies and suspension to exclusion from federal healthcare programs or referrals to other authorities. "Planned Parenthood and its affiliates have faced serious allegations involving the use of federal funds and compliance with federal law. Those allegations deserve a thorough review," Lankford said. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD "The HHS Inspector General should follow the facts, determine whether federal laws and funding requirements have been violated, and hold accountable anyone who has misused taxpayer dollars," he added. The push comes as the Small Business Administration (SBA) separately reviews more than $88 million in COVID-era Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans received by 38 Planned Parenthood affiliates. The lawmakers cited the SBA action in their letter, characterizing it as an investigation into whether Planned Parenthood affiliates "illegally received $88 million" in pandemic loans. SBA has described its action as a review of whether the affiliates were eligible for the loans. The review itself is not a finding that the affiliates violated the law. But the lawmakers want federal scrutiny to go well beyond the pandemic loans. PLANNED PARENTHOOD OFFERED HORMONES BUT HAD NO ANSWERS WHEN DETRANSITIONER SOUGHT HELP, UNDERCOVER PROBE FINDS They are asking the OIG to examine Planned Parenthood's broader HHS funding and coordinate with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) on what they described as a "comprehensive review" of the organization's activities. HHS-OIG told Fox News Digital Wednesday evening that it had not yet received the letter. "We have not received the letter and will review it for appropriate action once received," HHS-OIG said. Smith, co-chairman of the Congressional Pro-Life Caucus, said the scrutiny was "long overdue," citing allegations involving federal funding, reporting requirements, sexual exploitation and fetal tissue. FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP ADMIN OPENS NEW FRONT IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETING HEALTH INSURERS, DRUG MIDDLEMEN "It is long overdue for a comprehensive investigation and review, and I urge the HHS OIG to look closely to determine whether it has violated federal standards for federal funding recipients," Smith said. The congressional letter also points to reports alleging failures to comply with mandatory reporting requirements involving suspected child abuse or neglect. The lawmakers are asking federal officials to examine those allegations. They have not been established as findings by HHS-OIG. "Given the significant taxpayer resources that flow through federal health and human services programs, it is critical that recipient organizations operate with transparency, integrity, and full compliance with federal standards," the lawmakers wrote. The lawmakers closed by asking OIG to coordinate across the federal government to conduct a "comprehensive review" of Planned Parenthood's activities. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Thank you for your continued commitment to protecting the integrity of federal health programs and safeguarding taxpayer dollars," they wrote. Planned Parenthood did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Khanna eyes opportunity in Ocasio-Cortez plotting
articles.summary: As Democrats begin to position themselves for the 2028 presidential campaign, few contenders are being watched and analyzed as closely as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), whose decision to enter the race could alter the entire landscape of the Democratic primary. No one has more reason to observe Ocasio-Cortez’s every move than Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is frequently…
articles.body:
As Democrats begin to position themselves for the 2028 presidential campaign, few contenders are being watched and analyzed as closely as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), whose decision to enter the race could alter the entire landscape of the Democratic primary.

No one has more reason to observe Ocasio-Cortez’s every move than Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is frequently mentioned as the “other candidate in the progressive lane.”

If Ocasio-Cortez does stay out of the race — possibly deciding to run for a New York Senate seat instead — Khanna could have an opening as the party’s leading progressive candidate.

But if Ocasio-Cortez decides to run, it could complicate matters. For starters, the two lawmakers would compete not only for the same voters, but also for small-dollar donors and staff.

“AOC has the pole position in the race in the progressive field because she has the larger national following,” Democratic strategist Brad Bannon said. “But Khanna will get a big boost and have the advantageous progressive lane to himself if she puts her national ambitions on hold to run against Chuck Schumer in the New York primary.”

One progressive strategist said Khanna will “definitely” benefit if Ocasio-Cortez decides to sit out the 2028 race.

“There is a path for him regardless, but she’s sucking up a lot of oxygen right now, with the whole ‘will-she-or-won’t-she’ conversation,” the strategist acknowledged.

Behind the scenes, Khanna has been slowly moving toward launching a bid for the White House.

For months, he has been taking counsel from Ron Klain, the former White House chief of staff and respected party veteran. The New York Times reported that he has also brought in Julian Mulvey and Jeff Weaver, two longtime advisers to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who ran for president in 2016 and 2020 and held the progressive lane himself in those races.

Khanna told The Hill on Thursday he’s still strongly considering a White House bid.

He neglected to say whether he would benefit if Ocasio-Cortez didn’t enter the race but added, “We need a strong, competitive field with our best out there and see what meets the moment.”

“My vision is for economic renewal across America and the biggest economic project we have seen in generations,” Khanna said in a text exchange. “I have a roadmap for how to get the modern economy to enrich not just a few AI billionaires in my district, but the families I grew up with in Pennsylvania.”

For now, Khanna is focused on helping Democrats in the midterms, crisscrossing the country to appear at rallies. He has endorsed more than 70 candidates for House seats.

He has also become one of the most persistent voices in demanding the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, helping to lead a bipartisan push that forced the government to release some of the files.

He has also increasingly pushed forward a populist agenda, joining Sanders in proposing a 5 percent annual tax on billionaire wealth, which they said would raise trillions of dollars and help working and middle-class Americans.

Political observers say he’s also making big moves, telegraphing to the public that he’s taking his interest in running for president seriously and behaving like someone who is preparing to launch a campaign.

This summer, for example, he traveled to the Vatican as part of a congressional trip he led, discussing AI and safeguards with Pope Leo XIV.

He also traveled to Nevada, where he held a town hall with Hispanic voters and had a major swing through must-win Pennsylvania, where he was born. And he delivered a dose of tough love to the Democratic National Committee when he argued the party had lost its way while calling on Democrats to turn away corporate interests and embrace a more populist economic agenda.

Democratic strategist Basil Smikle said that because Khanna is less known, he would have to “make a case for that lane, which depending on timing, might be hard to do in a crowded field.”

While Khanna has been contemplating his political prospects, Ocasio-Cortez has been openly considering whether she’ll run for president. In recent days, she has traveled to upstate New York to campaign for candidates. Some have said the trips give a glimpse into what she might choose for her immediate future.

In an interview with The New York Times last month, Ocasio-Cortez sought to talk about the moment she faces, calling it a “very unique political window.”

“Oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said. “Life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

But she also expressed some personal hesitance: “I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life.”

Even if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t run, some Democrats expressed some skepticism on whether Khanna could own the progressive lane.

Democratic strategist Eddie Vale said while Khanna may try to own the left lane, “in a field this big, he will not have a clear hold on it like [Ocasio-Cortez] would.”

“He has done a good job getting attention as a congressman and bringing some fresh policy ideas forward, but it’s still a big leap for him to play at her level,” Vale said. “It’s like going to Broadway and seeing the understudy instead of the main character.”

articles.title: Younger candidates are finding it tough to break into Congress
articles.summary: More than 100 Generation Z candidates launched bids this cycle to run for Congress, per Future Caucus, but few have been successful. The attempts to run highlight how young adults are frustrated with partisan gridlock and want to enter the political sphere, even if their attempts are largely falling short. One possible reason for the…
articles.body:
More than 100 Generation Z candidates launched bids this cycle to run for Congress, per Future Caucus, but few have been successful.

The attempts to run highlight how young adults are frustrated with partisan gridlock and want to enter the political sphere, even if their attempts are largely falling short.

One possible reason for the lack of wins, says Layla Zaidane, president and CEO of Future Caucus, is that Gen Z candidates are more likely to run outside the two major parties, which makes it statistically harder to win.

“That mirrors the growing independence of Gen Z voters, and more broadly, that there are more people who are registering as unaffiliated,” Zaidane told The Hill. “When it comes to election day, we’re just seeing more Gen Zers fail.”

She added that these younger candidates tend to have less access to wealth and fundraising compared to more established ones.

“A lot of Gen Zers are running based on enthusiasm or some grassroots energy, but they aren’t as well-funded as their opponents,” she said.

Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist, knocked off long-time incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.) in a high-profile primary in Colorado’s 1st Congressional District earlier this year. She will almost certainly win the safely Democratic seat in November.

Unlike most other Generation Z candidates, Kiros had the money and the energy.

She fundraised more than $1 million, according to Federal Election Commission data, and boasted that her team made more than 500,000 calls and knocked on 100,000 doors while campaigning. DeGette still had more money than Kiros, as she had raised $1.6 million.

Adam Pennings, executive director of Run Gen Z, an organization that recruits and mentors young conservatives running for state government, told The Hill that it’s harder for Gen Z to break into high-level positions in Congress.

In addition to fundraising difficulties, young adults obviously lack the advantage of being incumbents.

Pennings said that Gen Z candidates can get on social media to raise awareness and money, but a broad social media following does not necessarily mean content will reach a specific constituent base.

“You are a young person and that is a benefit because you’re going to live with the consequences of your votes for 40, 50, 60 years,” Pennings noted.

Zaidane said that in previous elections, 1 in 6 candidates were under the age of 45, but now, it’s 1 in 3. “It includes more younger candidates, and that enthusiasm, appetite and choice to run in the first place is something that has been steadily increasing,” she added.

Although the majority did not advance past their primaries, there are still some Gen Zers whose names will appear on the November ballot.

In addition to Kiros, 29-year-old former Iowa state Rep. Joe Mitchell (R) is running for Congress against Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James in Iowa. The seat is currently held by Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate . Mitchell also co-founded Run Gen Z in 2020.

GOP candidate Michael Alfonso is 26 and married to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s daughter, Evita Duffy. He is running in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District, which is currently represented by Rep. Tom Tiffany (R), who is giving up his seat for a gubernatorial run .

And Riley Owen, a 27-year-old member of the Navy Reserve, is running as a Republican in Utah’s 1st Congressional District “to keep fighting for the American dream with results, not rhetoric,” according to his campaign website.

Joe Vogel, a 29-year-old Democratic delegate who represents Maryland’s 17th Legislative District, tried to run for a seat in the House in 2024.

“Being a young candidate has allowed me to have a platform both in my run for Congress and my run for the Legislature and the work I’ve been doing,” Vogel told The Hill.

He credits his loss in the 6th Congressional District’s 2024 primary to Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-Md.) for making him a better legislator and giving him a broader perspective of the state’s communities.

“One of the misconceptions that I think folks have about young candidates is that we only appeal to young voters, and that’s not the case,” Vogel said. “In both of my campaigns, we really built a multigenerational movement of folks.”

“We’re looking to turn the page and elect a new generation of leaders who would bring new ideas and a fresh perspective to the issues and a new sense of energy and enthusiasm for the work that needs to be done,” Vogel continued.

He argues that Gen Z has a chance to fix what older generations have done while giving future politicians something to look up to.

“Generations to come will look at this moment in time right now and ask, ‘What did they do, how did they meet this moment?’” Vogel said of Gen Z’s involvement.

Above all, this election’s losses have not discouraged young adults. Gen Z candidates have a sense of “I don’t need to wait my turn,” according to Zaidane.

When younger candidates come into the national spotlight, they’re often seen as having extreme positions. In reality, Zaidane said, they’re more passionate.

“The fact that so many of them are running outside the traditional true party system tells us that there’s a lot more nuance in their views and the issues that they’re running on than you might assume,” she said.

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com , jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

articles.title: GOP senators warn Trump is hurting Republicans with independents
articles.summary: Senate Republicans say President Trump has become increasingly toxic with independent voters critical to winning Senate races in battlegrounds such as North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Some GOP senators are warning Trump to stay away from key Senate races, cautioning that his presence would likely turn off independent voters. But vulnerable incumbents such as…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans say President Trump has become increasingly toxic with independent voters critical to winning Senate races in battlegrounds such as North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska.

Some GOP senators are warning Trump to stay away from key Senate races, cautioning that his presence would likely turn off independent voters.

But vulnerable incumbents such as Republican Sens. Roger Marshall (Kan.) and Jon Husted (Ohio) want Trump to visit anyway, hoping he’ll boost lagging enthusiasm among MAGA and GOP base voters.

Trump has urged Republican voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot in the midterm elections, but some GOP senators say that’s a risky move that could backfire with independent voters, whom they view as critical to keeping their Senate majority.

“Forty percent of our electorate is unaffiliated. You can’t win with just a pure MAGA base,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), whose seat in North Carolina is a big prize on the Senate battleground map.

Tillis, who is retiring, said Michael Whatley, the Senate Republican candidate in North Carolina, shouldn’t campaign with Trump before Election Day.

“I don’t think it benefits him. I haven’t seen any poll where [Trump] is going to help us with unaffiliateds,” he said.

Tillis said Whatley and other GOP candidates in toss-up races would be “smart” to create some distance from Trump, who registered a 24 percent job approval rating among independent voters in a nationwide Fox News poll conducted Sept. 11-14.

“If you’re going to be smart, you got to let the candidates be who they are,” the retiring senator said. “If they are concerned with the progress of the war in Iran, which most members are, or if they’re concerned with affordability … I think there are votes to be had by saying, ‘We got to work on this.”

An AARP-sponsored poll of 1,115 likely voters in North Carolina conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research from Sept. 17-20 found that only 26 percent of independent voters give Trump a favorable job performance rating.

The Hill reached out to the White House for comment.

Trump is planning to stump in several Senate battleground states before the Nov. 3 election, including Ohio, Iowa, Nebraska, Alaska, Texas and Florida.

Trump is planning to visit Ohio on Tuesday to support Husted, the embattled Senate GOP incumbent.

But some Republican senators think that Trump’s visit could backfire on candidates such as Husted or Iowa’s GOP Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson, who has recently stepped up her criticism of the Iran war and its impact on gas and food prices.

One Republican senator, who requested anonymity to comment on Trump’s plans to stump in Senate battlegrounds, argued it would be a mistake to campaign in Midwestern states where higher costs caused by the Iran war and Trump’s tariff policies are fueling voter anger.

“He will energize our base, and that’s important. We need our voters to turn out, but the ones that are making the decision, really, are those independent voters. And right now, they’re not looking favorably at President Trump,” said the GOP lawmaker.

The senator said the number of independents who are likely to be put off by Trump campaigning in a swing state are likely larger than the number of Republican voters who would be spurred to vote because of his visit.

“We need those independents,” the senator warned.

But two vulnerable Republicans in Midwestern swing states told The Hill that they view Trump’s presence as more of an asset than a liability.

Husted said that he wants Trump to campaign for him, noting the president soundly defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in Ohio during the 2024 election, 55 percent to 44 percent.

“He won Ohio by 11 points,” Husted said.

Marshall, who faces a surprisingly tough challenge from charismatic megachurch pastor and Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, said he would “love” it if Trump stumps for him in Kansas.

Marshall told reporters last month that he views Trump as critical to turning out GOP votes.

“There may be 200,000 people in Kansas that only vote when President Trump is on the ballot,” he said. “Certainly he needs to communicate to them that he is on the ballot, that if we lose the House it will just be one impeachment after another — his agenda is over with.”

Ford O’Connell, a GOP strategist and former Trump campaign surrogate, argues that candidates who do a better job of turning out core supporters will win in November.

“Trump is the best person at lighting a fire under the backsides of Republican voters to turn out votes. He is a one-man get-out-the-vote machine particularly among Republicans,” he said.

“The problem is making sure you get Republicans to be fired up if you want to hold many of these seats, particularly the ones that are in more traditionally red territories,” O’Connell added.

Trump is scheduled to travel Tuesday to Nebraska, where Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) is in a tough race with Independent candidate Dan Osborn, who has hit the GOP incumbent over data centers and his profitable stock investments.

Trump is also scheduled to visit Republican strongholds in the next few days, such as Oklahoma, Alabama and Texas.

“The president’s own numbers are not what they used to be, even in ruby-red Texas. And so making the election about him, pretending that his name is not on the ballot is not necessarily helpful if you’re downballot,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

“The usual argument is in circumstances like this you need to localize the race, not nationalize it. But the president seems determined to make the election about him at a time when you got $6-plus diesel prices and high gas prices,” he said.

Cornyn’s seat is up for grabs in the Lone Star State’s heated Senate contest between Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) and state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Senate GOP nominee.

Paxton, who defeated Cornyn in a primary earlier this year, was recorded telling a group of conservative donors and lobbyists last week that September’s GOP-held midterm convention in Dallas — which starred the president — hurt his poll numbers.

Asked if Trump is a drag on his candidacy, Paxton acknowledged: “When we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

The audio recording was reported by The New York Times.

A spokesperson for Paxton, however, disputed the notion that the Texas attorney general thinks Trump is weighing down his candidacy as “manipulated nonsense.”

Several recent polls show Talarico leading Paxton, even though Trump carried Texas with 56 percent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election.

A Marist University poll of 1,139 registered voters in Texas conducted from Sept. 17-20 showed that only 29 percent of independents in the state have a favorable impression of the president.

The same poll showed Trump with an overall approval rating of 41 percent and Talarico leading Paxton by 6 points, 50 percent to 44 percent.

articles.title: Trump’s powerful new friends are making MAGA uncomfortable
articles.summary: President Trump’s appearances with Chinese President Xi Jinping, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and leaders from Silicon Valley risk turning off his political base just as Republicans are seeking to turbocharge turnout ahead of the midterms, say GOP strategists. The president has always loved meeting with the powerful, even if they are dictators…
articles.body:
President Trump’s appearances with Chinese President Xi Jinping, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and leaders from Silicon Valley risk turning off his political base just as Republicans are seeking to turbocharge turnout ahead of the midterms, say GOP strategists.

The president has always loved meeting with the powerful, even if they are dictators or democratic socialists, as it makes headlines and highlights his own stature.

Trump was the first president to meet with North Korea leader Kim Jong Un, and he met with Russian President Vladimir Putin last year. He had a memorable buddy-buddy term in the Oval Office with Mamdani last November, even as his party sought to vilify the liberal mayor.

To many Republicans, the latest meetings are a danger.

“Frankly, it’s inexplicable,” one unnamed Republican strategist said. “Not because as president you shouldn’t meet with the Chinese president or event the mayor of New York, but given their toxicity with the base that you were desperate to try to turnout at higher than normal levels to try and offset your vulnerabilities with every other layer of the November turnout populace.”

“You need to fire up your base and instead you’re kind of deflating them in the homestretch,” the strategist added.

Trump hosted his Chinese counterpart last week for a lavish state visit at the White House. That meeting came after Mamdani hosted Trump at Gracie Mansion in New York City.

On Tuesday, Trump invited several tech leaders to the White House for a luncheon on artificial intelligence before appearing with them on the White House North Lawn for an impromptu news conference.

Polling shows that the president’s base views China with skepticism.

A July public opinion survey released by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that only 36 percent of MAGA Republicans said the U.S. “should undertake friendly cooperation and engagement with China” and that 63 percent said the U.S. should “actively work to limit the growth of China’s power.”

Influential MAGA figures such as former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have referred to leaders in Big Tech as “oligarchs” and have warned against unchecked artificial intelligence and data centers.

As for Mamdani, MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans have sought to make the New York City mayor the face of the democratic socialist movement as they seek to paint Democrats across the board as far left and extreme.

The GOP effort has made Trump’s publicly warm relationship with Mamdani more eyebrow raising. Still, polling shows there is somewhat of a populist overlap when it comes to both leaders’ bases.

Nine percent of 2024 Trump voters in New York City who voted in last year’s mayoral election said they backed Mamdani, according to NBC News exit polling .

Trump’s longtime pollster and adviser John McLaughlin noted the base has not warmed to Mamdani and Xi and views the tech industry with skepticism but said the president’s voters acknowledge the meetings are a part of his job.

“Trump voters absolutely don’t like Mamdani or Xi and they don’t like it when Big Tech censors us or the way they bias their news against Trump,” McLaughlin told The Hill.

The pollster described the base’s views of the president’s meetings with Xi and Mamdani as “a necessary evil” and noted the base views tech leaders differently.

“As for Big Tech, some leaders they like, for example Elon [Musk]. Others like [Mark] Zuckerberg, who censored us in 2020 and helped [former President] Biden with drop boxes and mail-in ballots, they still don’t trust. However, the base remains rock solid in their support of President Trump and his goals,” McLaughlin said.

Others have described the base’s view of Trump’s meeting with the leaders as purely strategic.

“The base sees this as Trump putting his personality to use to try and win people over, and get them to come to his viewpoint,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist.

“They don’t trust those folks. They don’t believe that the president should give any ground to them generally, but they do sort of think that he’s putting on a charm offensive,” he continued.

Steinhauser also noted that Trump has a history of charming some of those he disagrees with, noting that Trump invited Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei to dinner at the White House Sunday evening after the tech leaders had voiced concerns about deregulating artificial intelligence.

When asked if there are concerns about how the president’s base views the meetings, a White House official said Trump “is always working on making good deals for the American people.”

Polls show Trump remains popular with his base.

An NBC News Decision Desk poll released last month showed Trump’s approval rating with MAGA supporters at 93 percent. Meanwhile, an Economist/YouGov poll released last month showed Trump with a 91 percent approval rating among MAGA voters, 79 percent among Republicans, and 75 percent among voters who supported him two years ago.

“No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the President understands how to communicate with them,” said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, referring to Trump as the “the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.”

When asked whether his meetings with Xi, Mamdani and the tech leaders would depress the base, Steinhauser said Trump’s meetings with Big Tech could potentially be a drag on the base.

“The base knows and dislikes those Big Tech companies and leaders. That can be tied more directly to policies they don’t like,” Steinhauser said.

“There’s just a different, visceral reaction because the tech stuff is so tied to specific concerns that they have right now about the data centers, the financial bubble related to all of that, threats to their own jobs and well-being in a much more direct way,” he said.

articles.title: Trump clashes ahead as new Supreme Court term begins
articles.summary: The president has lost major cases and openly criticized the justices, but he still has a winning record at the court, which will consider his immigration policies and more this term.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s harsh criticisms may still be ringing in the ears of Supreme Court justices when they return to the bench for a new nine-month term next week. In the final months of its previous term and over its summer break, the conservative-majority court, which includes three Trump appointees, ruled against Trump on some of the issues he holds most dear. The justices blocked his sweeping tariffs, ended his plan to curb birthright citizenship, prevented him from firing a member of the Federal Reserve and blocked his plan to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of this fall’s election. The Supreme Court has “let our country down,” Trump said in a Truth Social post after the mail-in ballots ruling. The very justices he appointed — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — are “a shell of their previous selves,” he added. The president made similar claims in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, saying: “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often.” The president still desperately needs justices’ votes when key parts of his agenda come before the court in the coming months, in particular multiple cases arising from his hard-line immigration crackdown. The court could also weigh in on his administration’s ban on transgender people in the military, which the justices in a previous decision allowed to go into effect. Another appeal is pending in Trump’s effort to overturn a defamation verdict against him in a case brought by writer E. Jean Carroll, who accused him of sexual abuse. The court in June rejected an earlier Trump appeal concerning a separate case that Carroll won. Trump’s complaints about the court mask the fact that the administration has had plenty of wins, in particular in emergency cases that reach the court via what is known colloquially as the “shadow docket.” The court’s interim rulings have allowed the administration to move forward with immigration enforcement, restructuring of the federal government and even construction of a ballroom at the White House in emergency rulings while litigation continues. Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that overall “the administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful.” “President Trump will not stop implementing the America First agenda that he was elected on,” she added. The court resumes oral arguments Monday as it formally opens the new session, which runs until June, by hearing a major case about whether cities and counties can sue oil companies for the impacts of climate change. Those who regularly challenge Trump policies in court say their recent wins have them hopeful about this term, showing that even though the court has a 6-3 conservative majority, it is not a rubber stamp for the president. “Even with this court, you can go too far beyond the bounds,” said Norm Eisen, co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, which has challenged Trump on multiple fronts. The justices would not, for example, “allow Trump to hijack mail-in voting,” he added. Cecillia Wang, national legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union, was similarly relieved by some of the court’s recent decisions. “I think the court has proved it is willing to stand up to the Trump administration’s excesses. And that gives us confidence going into this term,” she said. Two key parts of Trump’s immigration policy are already lined up for Supreme Court review. In one, the justices will consider the administration’s ongoing efforts to deport immigrants to “third countries” they have no previous connection to if they cannot be returned to their home nations. The Supreme Court already allowed the policy to go ahead twice, suggesting the administration has a good chance of prevailing. The other case concerns the administration’s attempt to detain indefinitely thousands of people in deportation proceedings, a break from previous administrations, which would release those immigrants while their cases were adjudicated. Other Trump-related cases are likely to be added to the docket in time to be ruled on by next summer, with several appeals already pending. Among them is another potentially significant immigration case arising from the Trump administration’s shutdown of asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border. Lower courts ruled against the administration, although the policy currently remains in effect. Robert Luther III, who served in the White House during the first Trump term and is now a professor at Antonin Scalia Law School at George Mason University, said that, as with the previous term, much of the focus will be on Trump’s broad interpretation of executive power. “He’s always staked out an aggressive view of executive power. The court’s relationship with that view continues to unfold. Some of those cases he is winning and some he is losing,” he added. Although the court has been on its customary summer recess since the end of June, the justices have remained busy dealing with cases brought on the shadow docket. Such cases are typically dealt with swiftly, with no oral arguments or detailed written opinions. The shadow docket has increasingly become a key part of the court’s operations in recent years, with some of the rulings proving more consequential than those on the court’s traditional docket, in which the justices hear arguments and spend months deliberating before issuing long rulings. During the summer, the Trump administration filed seven shadow docket requests on a variety of issues. The court ruled for Trump on four of them and against him once, while one was withdrawn and one is pending. The administration’s most high-profile win of the summer recess allowed Trump to continue with his construction of a ballroom at the White House. But his single loss on his mail-in ballots executive order was a significant one, prompting some of his strongest criticism of the justices to date. Luther said the justices are likely able to put the president’s colorful rhetoric to one side. “I think the justices know the president is a politician,” he added. “I don’t think they take it personally.”
