articles.title: Iraq sounds alarm on terror threat from Syria one day after US troops leave
articles.summary: Iraq's foreign minister warns ISIS fighters could cross from Syria as Baghdad prepares its forces just one day after the U.S. military withdrawal.
articles.body: Iraq is preparing for the possibility that Islamic State fighters could spill across the border from Syria, the country's foreign minister said Thursday. It comes just one day after the U.S. military formally ended its counter-ISIS mission in Iraq. Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Thursday that Baghdad is closely watching recent ISIS activity in neighboring Syria, and warned that fighters crossing into Iraq could once again pose a threat to the country's security. "We are worried about ISIS activities inside Syria," Hussein said, adding that Iraqi forces were preparing to confront any movement toward the border. Still, he stressed that Baghdad believes its military can now handle the terrorist group without the large U.S.-led coalition presence that helped defeat ISIS's self-declared caliphate. ISIS POISED TO EXPLOIT HISTORIC US IRAQ EXIT, TERROR GROUP 'ACTIVELY WAITING IN THE GAPS,' EXPERT WARNS "If they would be capable to cross the border, that would be once again a threat to our security," Hussein said. "We are preparing ourselves – if there will be any movement from inside Iraq — to fight them and to defeat them." The warning came just after the departure of the final U.S. forces under Operation Inherent Resolve on Wednesday. US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS Trump hailed the withdrawal as a victory over ISIS, saying the terrorist group had been "completely decimated." "We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home," Trump said. "This day is a victory for the United States, a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over ISIS." But Hussein's warning came four days after Syrian authorities said they dismantled an ISIS cell operating across four provinces, arresting four of its leaders and seizing explosives that had been prepared for attacks. The cell had carried out kidnappings and was involved in assassinations and planting explosive devices, according to Syrian security forces. U.S. officials assess that ISIS has been severely degraded and no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq, but the terrorist group maintains scattered cells across Iraq and Syria. The Pentagon has said Iraqi forces are capable of suppressing the remaining threat themselves, while U.S. forces continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria aimed at preventing the group from reconstituting. The withdrawal marked the end of a U.S. military mission in Iraq that, in different forms, stretched across more than two decades and reshaped American foreign policy. The 2003 invasion toppled Saddam Hussein but gave way to years of insurgency and sectarian violence. Nearly 4,500 U.S. service members were killed before American forces withdrew in 2011. Three years later, U.S. troops returned as ISIS swept across large parts of Iraq and Syria, seizing Mosul and declaring a self-styled caliphate. The U.S. launched Operation Inherent Resolve in 2014, leading an international coalition that helped Iraqi forces reclaim the territory ISIS had captured. After the withdrawal, Iraq intends to pursue a bilateral security relationship with the U.S., though discussions on what that will look like have not yet begun. He said Baghdad and Washington had discussed the principle of a future security relationship while negotiating the coalition’s departure, but still need to work out the details, including what kind of training, intelligence sharing or other military cooperation could continue. At the same time, Baghdad is moving to bring Iran-backed militia groups operating outside the regular security forces under government control, another longstanding source of friction between Iraq and the U.S. Iraq had originally set a Sept. 30 deadline — coinciding with the U.S.-led coalition’s withdrawal — for armed groups to lay down their weapons or come under state authority. That deadline has since slipped to June 2027 as some powerful factions resist disarmament. Hussein said one group had issued a statement Thursday backing the government’s plan and another was expected to follow within a day, while negotiations continued with others. "A single group will not be allowed to take the decision in their hands and attack other countries," Hussein said. That question has taken on new urgency as Iraq tries to contain the fallout from the war between the U.S. and neighboring Iran. Hussein confirmed that a recent attack on Saudi Arabia originated from Iraqi territory near the Iranian border, prompting an investigation by Baghdad and consultations with both Riyadh and Tehran. Hussein said he had been in contact with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan over the attack and planned to visit Riyadh to discuss the matter further. The investigation remains ongoing, he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP More broadly, Hussein described Iraq as caught in the middle of the U.S.-Iran conflict, saying Iraqi territory had been struck by both sides. "We became a victim of this war," Hussein said. Baghdad has pressed both Washington and Tehran to resolve the conflict through negotiations, Hussein said, while seeking to keep Iraq from being drawn further into the fighting.

articles.title: Trump’s first-year government overhaul delivers change Washington hasn’t seen since the 1960s
articles.summary: IRS audit revenue dropped 35% after nearly 10,000 agents were let go, raising questions about whether federal workforce cuts are saving money.
articles.body: The Trump administration has reduced the federal workforce to the lowest point in roughly 60 years, according to newly released data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. As of August, just 2.67 million people were employed by the federal government, down from just over 3 million when President Donald Trump took office, marking the lowest headcount since 1966, per the BLS. The administration has estimated those cuts will produce significant savings, with OPM projecting that its Deferred Resignation Program alone will save more than $20 billion a year. But the reductions have also come with costs. Revenue collected from IRS examinations fell 35%, from about $10 billion in fiscal 2024 to $6.5 billion in fiscal 2025, as the agency was undergoing steep workforce reductions that ultimately cut examination and collection staffing by nearly 10,000 employees, according to a Treasury watchdog. APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS ORDER BLOCKING IRS FROM SHARING TAXPAYER DATA WITH ICE Former President Joe Biden secured nearly $80 billion in 2022 for the IRS over 10 years to upgrade its systems, improve taxpayer service and hire more staff, including enforcement personnel. The Trump administration has proposed further IRS cuts for 2027. Not all agencies have been hit the same by the Trump administration’s cuts. The Departments of Education, Agriculture and Housing and Urban Development have been cut particularly hard, whereas headcount at the Department of Homeland Security, which has been responsible for carrying out much of the president’s immigration agenda, has remained largely unchanged. TRUMP’S $5K CHECKS COULD JOIN STACK OF PAST UNFULFILLED PROMISES, FORMER CONGRESS BUDGET CHIEF WARNS Not included in the BLS’ count of government employees are the roughly 1.35 million members of the armed services or the approximately 100,000 people employed by intelligence agencies. Cutting the size of the federal workforce, a project that was eventually spearheaded by the Department of Government Efficiency and the Office of Personnel Management, was a major campaign promise during Trump’s 2024 run as he vowed to slim down what he said was a bloated government. OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT UNCOVERS $500M IN FRAUD AND WASTE IN FEDERAL HEALTH BENEFITS PROGRAMS GAO found that agencies spent about $6.7 billion paying employees who took part in the Deferred Resignation Program, which allowed many of them to stop working while still collecting a paycheck until they officially left government. The Partnership for Public Service also estimated the government spent $12.1 million rehiring workers who had previously been fired during the administration’s workforce reductions. Despite the cuts, most of which happened during the president’s first year in office, the Trump administration spent 3% more on federal salaries during its first year in power than the Biden administration did during its initial year. If Republicans win the midterm elections, the president has promised to cut $5,000 checks to all adult American citizens, a long-shot promise that, if followed through on, would cost the nation between $1.2 trillion and $1.35 trillion. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The White House did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Inside the House GOP's 4-week battle plan to save its majority
articles.summary: House GOP Chairwoman Lisa McClain reveals the four key topics Republicans plan to hammer home in the final weeks before the November midterms.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: House GOP leaders are quietly laying their battle plans for the final month ahead of the November midterm elections. A new memo being sent to Republicans across the country, first obtained by Fox News Digital, reveals four key topics that the House GOP is focusing on in the final four weeks before the election: the border, fraudulent use of taxpayer dollars, the economy, and public safety. "I think these are the points that the voters actually care most about," House GOP Chairwoman Lisa McClain, R-Mich., who leads Republicans' messaging strategy, told Fox News Digital. "[Democrats] want open borders. They want to defund the police, they want to take more money out of your pocket and give it to somebody else. They believe in bigger government. We believe in people... So those are the things that we're really hammering home during this election." It comes as Republicans fight an uphill battle to keep control of Congress for the latter half of President Donald Trump's final term. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. A recent Fox News poll found Democrats have a wider path to victory than Republicans in the House. Democrats are projected to win 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning the left only needs three more victories out of the 19 possible toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races. 10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY Republicans are also seeing political opportunity in the far-left insurgency that's gripped the Democratic Party during its primary cycle, warning that socialists are pushing the party further left than the majority of Americans. On the economy, which is a focus of week two in the GOP memo, Republican incumbents and candidates are encouraged to talk about "putting more money back in Americans' pockets and creating more opportunities to get ahead through hard work, ownership, and economic freedom." HOUSE CONSERVATIVES UNLEASH MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR MIDTERM BLITZ AGAINST DEM 'SOCIALIST' INSURGENCY The economy, including high grocery and gas prices, has become a central issue in the 2026 election cycle. Democrats have seized on Americans' struggle with cost-of-living as a political cudgel against Republicans, particularly using Trump's tariffs on allies like Canada and his war in Iran as arguments against the GOP. McClain acknowledged Americans' concerns, urging Republicans to be forthright with their voters but warning that Democrats' high-tax policies would worsen the situation. She also pointed to the low poverty rate and Trump's new trade deals as positives the GOP could highlight. "What we're not going to do is gaslight the American people, right? That's what the Democrats did, and it didn't work well for them," she said, referencing former President Joe Biden's handling of high inflation during his term. "But you have to take a look at the alternative. The alternative is absolutely terrifying." "We had a massive hole that we were digging out of under Biden. We have more work to do, of course we do, but do you want our trajectory, or do you want to go back to 9% inflation, open borders, and, and higher taxes? Because I tell everybody, every single Democrat voted to raise your taxes. They want more of your money." She echoed Trump's assurances that gas prices would drop when the conflict with Iran ended, adding, "We also don't want the number one state sponsor of terror to have a nuclear weapon, and we have to protect Americans from that." Meanwhile, Trump's polling is underwater, with the most recent Fox News survey from mid-September finding his disapproval rating at 61%. Trump's favorability remains a high 79% with Republican voters, however, meaning the GOP could still prevail by turning out the base on Nov. 3. One of the most decisive issues of his 2024 victory proved to be illegal immigration and the border, a fervor Republicans are hoping they can harness again come November. The memo encouraged Republicans to discuss "protecting America by stopping illegal immigration, enforcing our laws, and knowing who is entering the country." McClain pointed to policies promoted by far-left Democrats like abolishing police — and some mainstream Democrats' backing of sanctuary jurisdictions — as a contrast point for the election, while arguing Republicans were still supportive of legal immigration. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They tell you they want to defund the police. They tell you they want sanctuary cities. These are their words, not mine. These are the policies... they want," McClain said. "The Republicans, we want immigration, we believe in immigration, but we want people to come in the right way, and we darn sure want to make sure we know who's coming across."

articles.title: Furor grows over Cornell rape allegations
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Backlash to Cornell controversy grows ▪ FCC OK with Trump’s taxpayer-funded ads ▪ CNN blocked from White House press pool ▪ Fallout from a botched execution Outrage over the handling of an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 has reached a fever pitch this week, with Democrats calling…
articles.body:
▪ FCC OK with Trump’s taxpayer-funded ads

▪ CNN blocked from White House press pool

Outrage over the handling of an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 has reached a fever pitch this week, with Democrats calling for independent investigations as they slam the Trump administration for rolling back Title IX protections.

The investigation escalated Thursday night as New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed state Attorney General Letitia James (D) as special prosecutor to review the allegations.

A woman, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month against several defendants, including Cornell, the fraternity, the plaintiff’s own sorority, the men allegedly involved in the incident and the bar that served her. The lawsuit accuses seven men of sexually assaulting the woman over several hours at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 and includes a screenshot allegedly from that night of a man saying in a group chat that there is “free p‑‑‑‑ upstairs.”

Jane Doe went to the police nearly three weeks after the incident occurred, prompting investigations by the district attorney’s (DA) office and the university. Local prosecutors declined to press charges at the time, but the school kicked the fraternity off campus and doled out a range of punishments to the accused, including “expulsions and suspensions from Cornell.”

The DA’s office reopened an investigation Monday based on new information contained in the woman’s recent lawsuit. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has defended the office’s decision not to pursue charges at the time, saying the initial account from the woman didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, forced into sex or too incapacitated to be able to consent.

CBS News reported late Wednesday that it obtained a transcript of Jane Doe’s interview with a campus police officer weeks after the incident in 2024. The transcript revealed that the woman told the campus police officer that she could “say with 100 percent confidence I was raped,” and that she was “completely and totally incapacitated” before some of the sexual abuse occurred.

But she also appeared to differentiate between the initial sexual activity with two of the men, which she said, “I was pretty OK with,” and what happened later, when other men entered the room and allegedly became violent. She also said she had gaps in her memory and didn’t know how many people had sex with her that night, according to CBS News’s reporting of the transcript.

Van Houten told CBS News that he never saw the transcript of the woman’s interview when he declined to bring charges and instead relied on a statement written by a campus police officer that the woman signed.

But the handling of the case has left open some questions. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , a New York Democrat, said the allegations are “horrifying and deserve a thorough investigation that leaves no stone unturned.”

“There must now be a truly independent and exhaustive investigation — not only into what happened, but into how this case was handled from the moment she came forward,” he wrote on social media Wednesday.

New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D) similarly called the allegations “extremely serious and horrific” but said she was happy the DA’s office was reopening the case.

Hochul called this week for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case to “determine whether Cornell met every obligation to protect its students and pursue justice.” That same day, James launched an investigation into Cornell’s response to the incident.

Ithaca Mayor Robert Cantelmo condemned the school for its “appalling response” to the incident and for, at the time, having “failed to contact or coordinate any response with the Ithaca Police Department” and “hold the perpetrators to account,” he said in a statement .

Cantelmo announced an “immediate moratorium” on student event permits until Cornell “ conducts an accounting of its protocols to prevent and prosecute crimes of sexual violence and publicly releases new standards and practices to keep our community safe.”

On Capitol Hill, some Democrats have responded by criticizing the Trump administration, specifically highlighting the formal rollback this week of Biden-era Title IX protections, which included changes to rules governing the way schools address sexual assault complaints.

“The Trump administration has now made it harder for victims of sexual assault on college campuses to get justice with their cut to Title IX and their repeal of some of the Biden-era Title IX provisions,” Rep. Deborah Ross (D-N.C.), policy task force co-chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi .

articles.title: Why Trump might invoke the Insurrection Act before, during, or after the midterms
articles.summary: As midterm elections approach, concerns are growing that President Trump may attempt to nationalize voting or invoke the Insurrection Act to maintain power if Republicans face significant losses.
articles.body:
Midterm election polls suggest Republicans could lose control of the House and Senate . Meanwhile, President Trump, administration officials, and their media cheerleaders are identifying threats and offering scenarios that could justify a show of force or a national emergency declaration, potentially prompting the president to invoke the powerful Insurrection Act.

No president has ever invoked the Insurrection Act in connection with an election, but Trump could be the first. He already seriously considered invoking it twice, first in June 2020 during the George Floyd protests and again in January amid the ICE deportation confrontations and deadly shootings in Minneapolis.

The Insurrection Act authorizes the domestic deployment of the U.S. military or the federalization of the National Guard to suppress violent, out-of-control situations, such as rebellions, riots, protests, or insurrections. President George H. W. Bush last invoked it in 1992.

During his second term, Trump sought to normalize military deployments in six U.S. cities and threatened to do so in five more, citing the need to protect ICE agents during deportation arrests, secure federal property, and reduce crime , until courts repeatedly intervened .

From Trump’s perspective, mounting Republican fears of midterm losses might present a historic opportunity to use force , or even federalize the elections. The president knows that if Democrats control Congress, they will launch probing investigations that could cripple his final two years and threaten his legacy. With so much at stake, might Trump trigger an event like the 2021 Capitol riot?

The overarching reality is that our president does not lose elections. Losing signals weakness, which is not in Trump’s DNA, and clashes with his persona as the strongest, most powerful man in the world. However, his 2020 reelection loss, which Trump still insists he won, led to the Jan. 6 Capitol riots. The fallout from that catastrophe, along with the “stolen” election, continues to nag at his psyche and shape his political actions.

Although he is not on the 2026 ballot, Trump has personalized the midterms by asking South Carolina voters , “What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.” Still, if Republicans lose Congress, a legal loophole could prevent or delay the seating of the newly elected Democratic majority, possibly provoking a Jan. 6-type reaction.

Then consider a precarious pledge recited at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, with potentially dangerous consequences. President Trump led his loyal supporters in repeating , “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, …that I will go out [to vote] with my family, my friends. I’ll do it anyway, I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try and cheat like hell like they [Democrats] do.”

Then Trump asked, “You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell.” Concluding, “So please go and vote, because together we will defeat the communists.”

Has the significance of that pledge been downplayed? The president called all Democrats “communists” and urged cheating to defeat them. If the “communists” win, it would mean they cheated, and the election was rigged, stolen, or infiltrated by foreign voters, justifying Trump in declaring a national emergency, authorizing force, and potentially invoking the Insurrection Act.

No wonder state and local officials are preparing for election chaos. A July Gallup poll found 67 percent of adults are concerned about pressure on local officials to change election outcomes, 57 percent worry about properly handled ballots, and 52 percent cite fear of voter intimidation.

Throughout this year, the president has appeared cavalier about nationalizing voting, which could mean sending troops to secure voting places, protect ballot boxes, and oversee vote tabulation. In February, during Dan Bongino’s podcast, Trump said , “We should take over the voting, the voting in at least many — 15 places. The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting.”

Also in February, MAGA influencer Steve Bannon said , “President Trump has to nationalize the election… You’ve got to call up the 82nd and 101st Airborne [Divisions] on the Insurrection Act.”

In May, on Truth Social , Trump proclaimed that he would deploy an “Election Integrity Army in every single State to preserve the sanctity of each legal vote.” Soon, the Department of Justice will deploy 1,000 poll monitors.

This week, a stern directive from the secretary of Defense to protect and defend the election from “foreign actors,” coupled with recent statements by the FBI director and the secretary of Homeland Security signals a willingness to secure the election by force if there is a “threat” or “violation of the law” — exaggerated, imagined or manufactured by Team Trump.

From the military perspective, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine responded to questions from Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). His answers, in part, read: “The Joint Force has no plans to send federal military personnel or federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections … no plans to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material. I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.”

Note that Caine does not vow to resign if he were to receive such an order.

Watch this patriotic general because Caine’s actions could be the earliest signs of America’s first militarized election.

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill .

articles.title: 'DSA jihadi': LA mayoral candidate torched after defending 'genocide' comment during Jewish forum
articles.summary: Nithya Raman defended her use of "genocide" to describe Israel's actions in Gaza and backed the BDS movement at a tense Jewish community forum.
articles.body: Nithya Raman, the far-left Los Angeles mayoral frontrunner, defended her appearance on controversial streamer Hasan Piker's program and stood by her use of the term "genocide" to describe Israel's actions in Gaza when pressed by a Jewish audience Tuesday night, raising alarm among some Jewish voters. Raman's appearance before hundreds of attendees at a Jewish community mayoral forum quickly turned into a series of pointed exchanges over Israel, antisemitism and her past comments on the war in Gaza. Pressed over her appearance on Piker's show, Raman said candidates need to "meet people where they're at" and rejected the suggestion that appearing on his platform signaled an endorsement of his views. She also reaffirmed her use of the word "genocide" to describe Israel's actions in Gaza, saying she relied on unnamed "experts" who have used the same terminology. Both Raman and current Mayor of Los Angeles Karen Bass attended a candidate forum hosted by several Jewish organizations Tuesday evening, during which they were questioned on a range of topics but largely about antisemitism, public safety, homelessness, Israel and other issues of particular concern to the Jewish community ahead of the Nov. 3 election. FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER CALLED OUT BY MS NOW HOSTS IN FIERY EXCHANGE OVER HIM BEING A DRAG FOR DEMOCRATS "Nithya Raman's remarks should alarm every Jewish voter in Los Angeles," StopAntisemitism founder and Executive Director Liora Rez told Fox News Digital, arguing that "'meeting people where they're at' is not a defense" for appearing on Piker's program. The Wednesday night forum's moderator noted that many in the audience viewed Raman's appearance on Piker's show as "deeply hurtful," citing the streamer's past remarks about Jews and praise for groups including Hamas, Hezbollah and al Qaeda. Asked why she chose to appear and whether she worried it could be perceived as an endorsement of his views, Raman said she has consistently spoken out against antisemitism but believed candidates should engage voters across different platforms. ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES "I do believe that as an elected representative who's seeking higher office, you have to go and speak to voters," Raman said. "I think it's important for us as elected officials and as people running for office to go and speak to them even when you disagree with parts of those individuals... and meet them where they're at." Raman's explanation echoes a rationale Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed offered when defending his own appearances with Piker, arguing candidates should engage audiences on platforms where voters already are. DEM SENATE NOMINEE APOLOGIZES TO JEWISH VOTERS AFTER 'GENOCIDE' REMARK SPARKED BACKLASH The moderator then shifted to Raman's broader views on the Israel-Gaza war, noting that she had repeatedly described Israel's actions as "genocide" and asking her to define the term and address Jewish voters who viewed the language as deeply inflammatory. Raman acknowledged that "the word 'genocide' is a deeply painful word" and said she understood its historical significance, but maintained she used the term because other experts had done so and because she felt compelled to speak out after seeing "the targeting of hospitals" and "the deaths of children." FAMILY MEMBER OF LAWYER WHO COINED 'GENOCIDE' SEEKS TO STRIP NAME FROM GROUP ACCUSING ISRAEL OF ATROCITY "I have used that term, and I'm not an expert on these issues, and so I have looked to experts on these issues — international experts, Israeli experts — who have used that language, and that is what guided me in using that term in describing what's happening in Gaza," Raman said. But, in comments to Fox News Digital, Rez said "that charge is not supported by the facts," arguing "casualty figures supplied by Hamas-controlled authorities, often presented without distinguishing civilians from combatants, do not establish a deliberate campaign to destroy the Palestinian people." LA MAYORAL RACE HEADS TO NOVEMBER RUNOFF AS KAREN BASS FACES MAMDANI-STYLE SOCIALIST During the Tuesday night forum, Bass offered a sharply different view on the term and rejected its use in regard to the war in Gaza when pressed on the matter. Meanwhile, when asked where she differed from the anti-Israel positions of the Democratic Socialists of America, whose Los Angeles chapter has endorsed her mayoral campaign, Raman defended the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, as "a legitimate form of peaceful protest" before arguing that Israel-related issues were not part of her municipal platform and pointing to disagreements she has had with DSA on other issues. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA BACKS 'OUR TWITCH STREAMER' HASAN PIKER, RIPS ANTI-SOCIALISM HOUSE RESOLUTION Rez rejected Raman's characterization of BDS as "a legitimate form of peaceful protest," arguing the movement "is a discriminatory movement that singles out the world's only Jewish state for isolation and elimination." Local Los Angeles activist and Jewish mother of two, April Silverman, slammed Raman's appearance at the forum on X, arguing the mayoral frontrunner is not aware of "the concept of knowing your audience and reading the room." ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM "Nithya Raman couldn’t even pretend in front of a room full of Jewish Angelenos to be anything other than an antizionist radical," said Shana Meyerson, a podcast host who has a show called "The Unapologetically Jewish Podcast." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "She also doubled down on her 'genocide' accusations despite admitting she 'isn’t an expert,' and could not define what genocide is," Meyerson added. "Another DSA jihadi laughing in the face of Jewish Americans."

articles.title: Virginia should not make students choose between faith and financial aid
articles.summary: Religious college students in Virginia should not have to choose between following their religious calling and receiving the same educational assistance available to other students. That is the central issue in Hall v. Fleming, a case that presents the Supreme Court of the United States with an opportunity to correct a troubling anomaly in its…
articles.body:
Religious college students in Virginia should not have to choose between following their religious calling and receiving the same educational assistance available to other students.

That is the central issue in Hall v. Fleming , a case that presents the Supreme Court of the United States with an opportunity to correct a troubling anomaly in its First Amendment jurisprudence.

Virginia offers the Virginia Tuition Assistance Grant to eligible residents attending private, nonprofit colleges and universities in the Commonwealth. Eligible students can receive thousands of dollars toward their education. But Virginia draws a line when a student chooses certain religious majors.

Liberty University student Bethany Hall crossed that line and lost her grant.

Hall entered Liberty intending to study Music Education: Choral. She was initially approved for a tuition assistance grant. But during her freshman year, she “heard God’s call” to ministry and changed her major to Youth Ministries. That change made her ineligible for the assistance. She subsequently changed her major to Christian Leadership and Church Ministries and ultimately to Music and Worship. Those programs were likewise classified as ineligible religious programs.

Her choice of Music and Worship is particularly important. Hall is pursuing an education consistent with what she believes is her religious vocation: ministering through music and worship to young people. Rather than abandon that calling to preserve her financial aid, she chose to continue in the religious major. As a result, she has personally paid the tuition that the Virginia Tuition Assistance Grant program would otherwise have covered.

Had Bethany continued to pursue a degree in music education, she would be eligible. But because she is pursuing a degree in worship music, she is not.

That is precisely the kind of choice the First Amendment prevents. But, in 2004, in a case called Locke v. Davey, the Supreme Court said the opposite — that states can discriminate against students of faith in tuition assistance programs.

And Virginia’s program does exactly that. It does not simply ask whether a student attends an eligible institution. Students at religious universities can participate in the Virginia Tuition Assistance Grant program. Rather, the state examines what the student chooses to study and withdraws the benefit if the subject becomes something the state deems too religious. Under the program, religious training and theological education programs are excluded, even though students pursuing eligible and religious majors as a double major can remain eligible under certain circumstances.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit explained that Hall’s case is materially identical to Locke v. Davey. But one of the judges on the panel, Judge Richarson, filed an opinion arguing that Locke had been wrongly decided and called on the Supreme Court to take the case and overrule it.

Since Locke, the court has repeatedly strengthened protections against religious discrimination in government benefit programs. In Trinity Lutheran Church v. Comer, Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, and Carson v. Makin, the court made clear that government generally cannot exclude religious participants from otherwise available public benefits simply because of religion. Most significantly, Carson rejected the notion that government may evade the Free Exercise Clause merely by characterizing discrimination as a restriction on “religious use” rather than religious status.

That principle should apply to Bethany in this case. The government should not be in the business of deciding which academic pursuits are too religious to deserve financial assistance.

A student studying business, engineering, history, or music education does not surrender constitutional protection by switching to study ministry or worship. The First Amendment protects religious exercise precisely because government is not supposed to determine which lawful religious commitments are worthy of equal treatment and which are not.

Bethany’s case involves more than a modest tuition assistance grant. It asks whether government can condition an otherwise generally available benefit on a student’s willingness to abandon a religious calling.

The Supreme Court should grant Bethany’s petition, overrule Locke v. Davey, and reaffirm the simple constitutional principle that government may not tell a student that she can have a benefit if she gives up her faith, or keep her faith if she gives up the benefit.

Steve Fitschen is President of the National Legal Foundation . He is lead counsel in Hall v. Fleming.

articles.title: Minnesota’s Senate race could be Republicans’ November surprise
articles.summary: Republicans were smart to make welfare fraud a central issue in the midterm elections.
articles.body:
Republicans were smart to make welfare fraud a central issue in the midterm elections. How do I know? Because Michele Tafoya (R) could well become the first Republican senator from Minnesota since Norm Coleman left office in 2009. She is running on bringing much-needed accountability to the state’s scandal-ridden benefits programs .

“Unexpected” has long been the hallmark of Minnesota politics. Coleman became mayor of St. Paul in 1993 campaigning as a Democrat; he switched parties three years later to run as a Republican for the governorship but lost to pro wrestler Jesse Ventura . He finally won a Senate seat in 2002 but was then ousted by comedian Al Franken (D) in the blue wave presidential election of 2008. Clearly, almost anything can happen in the Gopher State .

Right now, Tafoya is trailing the Democratic nominee, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) by less than 2 points in the RealClearPolitics average of polls — within the margin of error. The sleeper race could absolutely determine which party ends up in control of the Senate.

Tafoya fits comfortably with Minnesota’s history of unorthodox candidates. She is a well-known broadcaster and commentator, having won four Sports Emmy Awards and set records for covering five Super Bowls and 327 NFL games, the “most national primetime games of any sideline reporter in league history,” according to her website. Her official bio quotes the San Francisco Chronicle famously calling her “widely recognized as the best sideline reporter in sports.”

Tafoya is attractive, smart and articulate, but she has never held political office. If covering sports is about highlighting who is playing by the rules, she is the perfect person to challenge Flanagan, who has served as Governor Tim Walz’s lieutenant since 2019.

Flanagan, described as a “ progressive ” by NBC News, beat out moderate candidate Angie Craig in the August Democratic primary. Voters should have known better, because Flanagan has baggage. Earlier this year, her boss, Walz decided against running for another term in the governor’s mansion, scurrying for cover after the massive scandal broke over multiple forms of benefits-fraud. Minnesotans were furious about the theft of as much as $9 billion of their taxpayer dollars, and they blamed the lax oversight on Walz, Flanagan and others in charge, who allegedly turned a blind eye .

The fraud was perpetrated by cheats (mostly) in the Somali immigrant community, who created bogus non-profits that were supposedly offering child care, health programs, school lunches and other vital services but instead cruelly pocketed the funds awarded by the state government.

Walz’s approval rating has plummeted over the last year as more information surfaced about the extent of the fraud, sliding from plus-19 net positive in June 2025 ago to minus-14 in August 2026. He has also been dragging Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison (D), Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D) and the state’s Democratic legislature down with him. Though separate numbers are not available for his lieutenant governor, she has almost certainly been tarnished as well.

Tafoya is hitting her opponent hard on the scandal, posting on X , for example: “Peggy Flanagan ignored warning signs while fraudsters stole our tax dollars. She has spent eight years as lieutenant governor in the Walz administration, yet now wants Minnesotans to believe she had nothing to do with its failures.”

State officials reportedly looked the other way as the money went missing, worried they might lose the Somali vote ; in fact, they ramped up even more taxpayer-funded handouts. Enabled by a rare Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta in state government, Walz pushed through universal free school meals and a state program for paid family and medical leave .

As a result, voters are not only swallowing the huge theft of tax dollars, they are also paying among the highest taxes in the country. Minnesota currently ranks 44th overall in the Tax Foundation’s state tax competitiveness index. It could be that voters have had enough.

Industrial-scale welfare fraud isn’t the only issue boosting Tafoya’s chances. In a small gathering recently in Manhattan, she noted that fewer than half of the kids in Minnesota can read or do math at grade level — a charge backed up by recent new data from the Minnesota Comprehensive Assessments . State education officials blamed disruptive deportations of illegal immigrants by the Trump administration for the weak test results, but that won’t hold up. Passing the buck is convenient politically, but it doesn’t explain why the state’s children performed almost as poorly the year before.

Minnesota also saw some of the worst rioting in the country during the 2020 protests against the George Floyd killing, with at least two people killed . Walz and Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey were criticized for acting slowly in response to the protests , allowing widespread destruction of hundreds of businesses.

Tafoya has vowed to work closely to make sure the police have the resources — and the laws — they need to keep Minnesotans safe. She has earned endorsements from the Minnesota Police and Peace Officers Association and other law enforcement agencies. She backs deportation of immigrants who are convicted of fraud, demands mandatory minimum sentences for fraudsters and calls to “strip federal funding from any state that refuses to implement anti-fraud controls or follow basic audit and recovery practices.”

This is smart politics. Americans don’t like being cheated.

One local news organization recently described the race as “quiet,” not attracting the tsunami of outside funding that Senate races in Texas or Maine, for example, are hauling in. Tafoya couldn’t be happier; running on reforming state governance after one of the biggest welfare scandals in U.S. history is working for her — as it should.

Just occasionally, politicians need to pay a price for not paying attention to the people who elected them.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] You did not, I hope, have to take any…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

You did not, I hope, have to take any notice of an empty online furor over Arkansas’s Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders ’s campaign ad that cast a young, white male as a welfare freeloader redeemed from sloth by work requirements.

Arkansas’s welfare recipients are overwhelmingly white , but it is true that they are slightly more female than male, owing to the high number of single moms who qualify for food assistance, Medicaid and other programs. Of course, no sane politician wants to run an ad bragging about kicking mothers off of welfare. And since the bad old days of the “ welfare queen ” stereotype of the 1970s, wise Republicans — especially Southern Republicans — have been careful about unfairly racializing the issue. If most beneficiaries are white, choosing a Black actor would be a deliberate provocation. So, good judgment would dictate that if you wanted to tell a welfare-to-work story, your imaginary beneficiary would be a white dude.

Some in the mainstream press called the backlash “conservative,” which is a funny way to talk about a bunch of very-online race obsessives having a conniption fit over a campaign ad posted online in Arkansas. It’s a relatively poor state — 28 percent of its residents are Medicaid recipients — and while it is still highly unlikely that it will be competitive in November, it might be prudent for an Arkansas Republican to address anger over unpopular cuts from President Trump ’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Selling welfare-to-work would seem to be the conservative answer, while bellyaching about race and gender issues is something else.

It’s not an important story, but I’m flagging it for you because it points to a significant problem confronting a Republican Party seemingly unable to grapple with what is shaping up to be an epic thrashing this fall: audience capture.

As a recent Wall Street Journal analysis revealed, the “manosphere” podcasters and other online right-wingers have been having a hard time finding new heroes and villains in a world where Trump is less relevant. While Trump mentions per hour (TPH?) have remained steady on left-wing shows at more than 35 per hour, the right-wingers can barely manage a dozen. That’s still a lot of Trump, but nothing like the highs of 2024 and 2025.

While the members of the president’s base — typically older, white, working-class voters — are with him always , the content-creation community and audience, which skew younger, more affluent and more radical, are looking for something else. Is it frustration over the interminable Iran war? Anger over a post-Minneapolis softening on immigration enforcement? The onset of lame-duck status as the GOP readies for a donnybrook in 2028? A tacit acknowledgment that the president is a drag on his party this year?

When even Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is saying it , there’s probably something to that last bit. The strategic choice for Republicans, therefore, would be to have the president busy himself with home decor projects, going to sporting events and planning parties and not make him any more a part of the midterm debate than necessary.

Or… take big bucks out of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) budget to fund campaign ads starring Trump himself. The lesson that the president apparently took from the fall of former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem is not that it is unwise and maybe illegal to use taxpayer dollars for self-serving campaign-style spots, but that those spots should have been about him instead of her. The president knows his base: people who watch TV, not 20-something bro stream viewers. Those guys are the heart of the future that Vice President Vance is hoping to build, but MAGA is still mainly for a linear audience.

However legally dubious and ham-fisted the approach, jollying up older adult voters who are feeling disillusioned about the president is not an insane strategy. In the same way that those right-wing podcasters are chasing their audience, so is the content creator in chief. For all of his mastery of Twitter in the dawning age of social media, Trump is a product and producer of television.

When asked about the leaked audio of Paxton blaming his crummy polling performance in his Senate race partly on Trump’s two-day telethon of a midterm convention in Dallas last month, the president did not rebuke Paxton or deny the story. He talked about the event’s TV ratings, repeating his ludicrous claim that it had more viewers than the NFL. The taxpayer-funded ads are essentially promos for the new fall season of the Trump show. It’s basically “Shovin’ Buddies.”

Trump’s whole political career has been a testament to the power and peril of audience capture. His intense bond with his voters/viewers has put him in the Oval Office twice, but his sensitivity to the preferences of his superfans makes him unable to lead in difficult moments. When there are no appealing answers, whether it’s on deportations, tariffs or a war with Iran, Trump loves the boffo ratings when the new program launches, but he gets squeamish when his fans tire of the storyline.

That’s part of why those right-wing content creators are tuning out Trump’s storylines. The president is focused on burnishing his own image and legacy by making things seem better than they are, which might be of some ancillary benefit to Republicans. The very online right, though, needs dragons to slay, which means identifying (or inventing) dangers to their audience. Defending a struggling president is a bore and a ratings killer. Outrage and panic work wonders, though — whether that’s the unbearable whiteness of imaginary welfare recipients, the anxiety about brown skin in burnt orange or the problem of women scrolling without supervision .

Much like the fevers of the very online left drove the Democratic Party batty in the “Woke 1” era, the boutique interests of click-obsessed weirdos are steering Republicans toward a cliff. Normal, persuadable voters mostly don’t know about these things, and if they do, they would probably find the obsessive focus on race and gender by these influencers to be creepy and un-American. But the ravening maw demands content, so content it shall have.

Which brings us to a signal moment of the 2026 midterms: The swan dive Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) took in a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing this week with former prosecutor Jack Smith . He wanted the Army-McCarthy Hearings but ended up with a Charlie McCarthy routine .

The world has dumped enough scorn on the story of how laziness and arrogance led Schmitt, a former prosecutor himself, into such a colossal blunder. The fact that this little item touting Schmitt’s own “buzz” as a possible 2028 running mate to Vance was placed to run on the day that the senator was preparing for his big “dirtbag” moment tells us a great deal about what the Missourian had in mind for the hearing. Schmitt wanted content more than he wanted to be a diligent lawmaker, as evidenced by the choice he made .

Schmitt will probably not pay much of a price for his blunder. By the time that he is up for reelection in 2028, voters in very red Missouri won’t care about the stumble. And the idea that Republicans will be nominating a ticket with two hard-edge, Roman Catholic, nationalistic, middle-aged, white guys from the Midwest was going to be a very iffy proposition whether Schmitt had memed himself or not. If Vance is the nominee, as expected, he will be in the market for a great deal of softening and gravitas as he looks for a running mate.

But, like the umbrage over the Arkansas ad, the Schmitt episode still provides a tight example of one of the biggest obstacles to effective governance in the 2020s.

Audience capture is a problem that afflicts both parties. It is a function of a splintered media world, the distortive effects of partisan primary elections and lazy politicians. Persuading voters is hard. Pleasing the loudest voices is easy, by comparison. Running around and pandering to politically obsessed content creators and consumers is no doubt a drag, but it isn’t very risky. Ask Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) what happens to politicians who get caught being too good at their jobs. The monetized online mob will sooner or later take you out.

Cornyn’s potential successor, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico , has already been put on notice by the left-wing content king, Hasan Piker , that if Talarico doesn’t pander, there will be consequences : “We have to remind him that we are the force that backed him early on, and we are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power.”

That word Piker used, “allowed,” speaks to a great deal of what has wrecked American politics and government. It’s supposed to be voters, not Twitch streamers or social media click farmers, who allow leaders to have power.

Audience capture is badly limiting Republicans’ options for mitigating their losses in November, just as it will presumably limit Democrats’ options for winning the presidency in 2028. When the content creators win, everybody loses.

On Tuesday, Jackson said it is ‘unfortunate’ that members of the Jewish community in his state do not call the ongoing conflict in the Gaza Strip a ‘genocide.’ ‘It’s unfortunate that there are people here in Maine that don’t like to use that term, only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust,’ he said in an interview with News Center Maine. Jackson also said that ‘senseless murders, horrific murders, are happening to both sides’ of the conflict between the Israeli and Palestinian people, specifically criticizing Hamas. … Susan Collins has voiced concerns for the treatment of both Palestinians and Israelis in the ongoing conflict, but she has previously stopped short of calling it a ‘genocide.’ The senator has also been a staunch advocate for Israel’s ‘right to defend itself’ in the past.”

Failure to do so could make winning impossible. The challenge is not unique to Mr. Talarico. In recent years, Democrats have watched with dismay as Black voters showed signs of drifting away from the party, either staying home or, in 2024, voting for President Trump.”

Farmers could thresh Republican chances in the Plains, Midwest: The Wall Street Journal : “With just over a month to go until midterm elections, Republicans are facing the worst political environment in farm country in decades. Tariffs and high prices for diesel, gas and fertilizer because of the war in Iran, along with President Trump’s plans to import more beef, have soured the moods of America’s farmers and ranchers, giving an opening for Democrats in what are typically solid red states. articles.title: Trump pushes Senate Republicans on ‘No More Changing of Clocks Act’
articles.summary: President Trump is ramping up pressure on Senate Republicans to move forward with legislation making daylight saving time permanent, blaming Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) for holding up the bipartisan effort to end the twice-a-year changing of clocks. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which Trump has dubbed the “No More Changing of Clocks Act,”…
articles.body:
President Trump is ramping up pressure on Senate Republicans to move forward with legislation making daylight saving time permanent, blaming Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) for holding up the bipartisan effort to end the twice-a-year changing of clocks.

The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which Trump has dubbed the “No More Changing of Clocks Act,” in July with a 308-117 vote, but the measure has yet to clear the Senate.

“A ridiculous Clock changing process that takes place twice a year, costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine,” Trump wrote in a lengthy Truth Social post early Friday.

“People don’t want to go around changing their Clocks anymore and, besides, far and away, most people like having an hour of extra sunlight in the evening, rather than in the morning,” he added.

Trump singled out Cotton, whose reelection bid he endorsed, saying the bill was being “held up” by the Arkansas Republican “for reasons unknown.”

The senator has been among the most vocal opponents of permanent daylight-saving time, warning that later winter sunrises would leave children heading to school and millions of Americans traveling to work in the dark.

“If permanent daylight savings time becomes the law of the land, it will again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans,” he said last year.

Trump argued that more evening daylight would help reduce crime and traffic accidents, while benefiting public health and industries including sports, tourism, restaurants and retail.

“People are sick and tired of having to change their Clocks twice a year. Even most farmers would rather have additional time in the evening to harvest their crops,” Trump wrote, adding that the issue is one Republicans, Democrats and independents can agree on.

He added, “It is foolish, inconvenient and, in some cases, very costly.”

Congress moved most of the country to year-round daylight-saving time in early 1974 in response to the energy crisis, records show .

But the experiment quickly ran into opposition as winter sunrises came later and concerns grew over children traveling to school before daylight. Lawmakers ended the experiment that fall.

The Senate unanimously passed a similar bill in 2022, but it stalled in the House.

This time, the lower chamber of Congress has acted while the proposal faces uncertainty in the upper chamber. Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also cast doubt on whether the measure can secure the 60 votes needed to advance.

articles.title: California mayor accused of drunken behavior, racial slur, harassment in chief of staff's claim
articles.summary: Berenice Ballinas accuses Anaheim Mayor Ashleigh Aitken of using a racial slur, questioning her sexuality and appearing intoxicated at city events.
articles.body: Anaheim Mayor Ashleigh Aitken has been accused of repeatedly appearing intoxicated during city-related events, making racially derogatory remarks and asking intrusive questions about sexuality, according to a newly released 25-page government claim. Berenice Ballinas, who has worked in Aitken's office since December 2022 as her chief of staff, alleges harassment, discrimination and retaliation based on her perceived sexual orientation, Mexican heritage and Catholic faith. The filing also accuses the city of failing to adequately respond after concerns were raised. Ballinas outlines a number of alleged incidents involving Aitken, including accusations about the mayor's conduct while drinking. SMALL-TOWN VIRGINIA MAYOR REPORTEDLY ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY SHOWING UP DRUNK TO TRAIN DERAILMENT She alleges that Aitken arrived at a City Council meeting in April 2025 appearing "visibly impaired by alcohol." After a closed session at the meeting, Ballinas says she ultimately drove Aitken home in then-City Manager Jim Vanderpool's city vehicle. During the roughly 15-minute ride, the claim alleges Aitken began searching through Vanderpool's vehicle and personal belongings and taking photographs with her cellphone. Ballinas says she objected and told the mayor to delete the photos because Vanderpool's information was private. Aitken is also accused in the claim of making racially derogatory remarks. Ballinas alleges that Aitken made multiple derogatory comments concerning her Mexican heritage and referred to her as a "dirty Mexican." During a separate incident at Disneyland in May 2025, Ballinas said she offered to drive Aitken after believing the mayor was too intoxicated to drive home safely. However, Aitken allegedly declined the offer because she refused to have "a Mexican" drive her, according to the claim. Aitken has directly denied using the racial slur attributed to her and said the allegations deserve to be investigated. REPUBLICANS TURN ON HOUSE GOP LAWMAKER ACCUSED OF LATE-NIGHT TEXTS, LAVISH GIFTS TO FEMALE STAFFERS "These allegations are extremely serious, and they deserve to be investigated. I did not use the racial slur attributed to me, and I have always been a champion of the LGBTQ community," she said in a statement posted last month on Facebook. Fox News Digital has reached out to Aitken's office for comment. Ballinas also described alleged conduct during a team dinner, where she said she observed Aitken becoming "physically affectionate" with another person, including touching and grabbing him, resulting in the mayor's husband removing her from the event. While walking back toward the hotel, Ballinas alleges Aitken became angry and knocked or pushed over a bicycle, damaging its mirror, before later falling in the street. Aitken then fell in the street, according to the claim. When Ballinas told the mayor's husband that Aitken was not OK and needed help, he allegedly responded, "Don't we all?" ANOTHER TOP SEATTLE MAYORAL AIDE EXITS AS KATIE WILSON ADMINISTRATION FACES CONTINUED STAFF TURNOVER The filing says Aitken's husband later asked Ballinas to make a Venmo payment to compensate the bicycle's owner. Ballinas also makes several allegations concerning questions about her perceived sexual orientation. She said Aitken took her to Disneyland's Club 33 for a birthday lunch on June 10, 2026, where the mayor consumed alcohol and repeatedly questioned whether Ballinas was a lesbian. Later at the 1901 Lounge, Aitken allegedly questioned a Disney cast member about whether he was gay or straight and about his dating life. Disney later sent written correspondence to the Club 33 member whose membership was used for the visit, saying cast members had reported "rude, insensitive, and inappropriate remarks" during the outing. The government claim says Ballinas was forced to take leave beginning around July 31 and alleges retaliation after she reported or opposed conduct she believed violated laws or workplace rules. Anaheim has said a review of the allegations is underway. Aitken has pledged to participate in the process. articles.summary: Democratic candidate Sharice Davids argues that current Republican policies on healthcare and agriculture have betrayed rural communities, prompting new Democratic leadership bids in states like Iowa and North Carolina.

MAGA politicians promised “to put rural America first.” But, after two years of complete Republican control, rural communities are experiencing betrayal after betrayal. While rural Americans struggle to make ends meet, Washington insiders and corrupt politicians have gutted our health care system, sent costs soaring, and put our agriculture industry on the brink of collapse.

To pay for massive tax breaks benefiting the wealthiest few, Republicans in Washington are systematically devastating our nation’s rural health care system. Their Big, Ugly Bill ’s massive cuts to Medicaid put hundreds of rural hospitals and clinics at risk of closure, with some communities already experiencing closures .

In Kansas, this law has strained the 58 percent of rural hospitals that are already at risk of closing. Losing a hospital or clinic is devastating for rural communities, forcing patients to drive miles more to see a doctor while eliminating jobs from local economies. Despite warnings from healthcare providers and concerns from families and communities across the country, these cuts moved forward.

President Trump’s chaotic and failing trade war has wreaked havoc on our farmers. More than 70 percent of farmers report they cannot afford the fertilizer they need to grow their crops. Prices for tractors, harvesters and other critical agricultural equipment are spiking under the tariffs. Tariffs have also depressed commodity prices by cutting farmers off from some of their biggest customers.

Then, to add insult to injury, Trump’s reckless war in Iran, which I voted to end, has led to skyrocketing diesel prices , squeezing farmers’ already tight margins. This all while the administration cuts staffing at the agencies meant to support everyday farmers and pretends a temporary bailout will address their concerns, leaving many struggling to receive the basic services they pay for. It’s no wonder that farm bankruptcies are at a six-year high .

In Kansas, these extreme decisions in Washington have hit our communities especially hard. In addition to rising costs on everything and cruel cuts to our health care system, our state’s cattle ranchers have twice been undercut by the Trump administration greenlighting imports of now-recalled Argentinian beef and gutting the agency that could have prevented the screwworm outbreak.

Rural communities are looking for relief, and Democrats are focused on substantive ways to deliver it. In working to earn every vote in every corner of the country, Democrats are offering a forward-looking vision for rural communities, one where all Americans who work hard and play by the rules can achieve the American Dream.

That vision includes repealing the reckless tariff-taxes, ending the war in Iran, and restoring healthcare funding to our rural communities. While Democrats put forth plans to make life better for everyday Americans, extreme Republicans in Washington continue to push for more healthcare cuts and starve rural communities of the critical funding and services they rely upon.

In Iowa, whose rural communities have been hit hard by rising costs and challenges facing healthcare and agriculture, voters there are looking for change and representation from leaders laser-focused on making their lives better: lowering costs, protecting healthcare and public health , and sustainably supporting their state’s farmers, without solely relying on temporary bailouts .

In next month’s election, I am confident Iowans will elect Lindsay James for Iowa’s 2nd District, Christina Bohannan for Iowa’s 1st District, and Sarah Trone Garriott for Iowa’s 3rd District who will be champions for working Iowans — not just a rubber stamp for the corrupt Washington insiders.

In western North Carolina, communities are struggling to afford everyday necessities while still reeling from Hurricane Helene. Many residents continue to wait for the federal support they need to rebuild, leading Jamie Ager in North Carolina’s 11st District, a fourth-generation farmer, to challenge the broken government by running for office. In Congress, Ager will put western North Carolina first, working to strengthen hurricane recovery efforts, lower costs, and revitalize rural small businesses.

Rural communities deserve to know that Democrats are listening, showing up, and fighting for them. We are making historic investments to build trust within rural America and recruiting candidates whose backgrounds and experiences reflect the districts they are running to represent.

Rural communities are the heart of America, and they deserve a government that understands their way of life and will put their interests first. Democrats are taking no vote for granted and will continue to show up in every corner of this country to build a durable House majority.

Sharice Davids represents the 3rd District of Kansas and is a member of the House Agriculture Committee.
